625203,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.1.1.1,1922-04-24,,,,stagedirection,,,,"Mr. DONALD M. KENNEDY (West Edmonton) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 54 to amend the Criminel Code. He said: This is a bill to repeal section 20 of Chapter 25, the statutes of 1921. This section of the Criminal Code was passed in June of last year, in the face of an insistent demand from a part of the West for an investigation into alleged frauds in connection with the transfer and location of half-breed scrip. Many frauds complained of are supposed to have been committed as far back as fifteen years ago, and the amendment, section 20, Chapter 25 of 1921, provides that prosecution cannot be taken after three years from the commission of the offence.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.",,,,

625205,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.2.1.1,1922-04-24,,,,stagedirection,,,,"Mr. JOSEPH ARCHAMBAULT (Cham-bly and Vercheres) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 55, an Act to revise and amend the Naturalization Act, 1914. He said: This is a bill to amend the Naturalization Act of 1914. By this act, a residence of five years, in the previous eight years, in His Majesty's Dominion was required, with one year, the last year, in Canada. When the war broke out an amendment was enacted which provided that the time spent overseas in the crown forces by those who enlisted would count as residence in Canada, but there was no provision for men who enlisted in the armies of the allied countries. The result is that if a Belgian, a Frenchman or an Italian who was a resident in Canada before the war, and who had spent four years in Canada, enlisted in the allied army, his time while he was overseas did not count, and when he came back to Canada, say in 1919, he had to reside in Canada five years more in order to obtain naturalization papers. I submit that this was an oversight causing a grave injustice, and the purpose of my bill is to remedy that injustice. I will explain the bill fully on second reading.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.",,,,

625288,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.9.1,1922-04-24,ee1cc492-9867-48d3-a612-c1fb491d2916,ca.m.1883,Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Centre Winnipeg) moved:,,THE UNEMPLOYMENT SITUATION,,,That, in the opinion of this House, in view of the widespread unemployment with which the Municipalities and Provinces find themselves unable to cope, it is desirable that the federal Government should devise some means of dealing effectively with the situation.
He said:
column2: This resolution deals with a

column1: question that is of vital importance to Canada at the present time. It was a matter of regret to a great many of us that in the Speech from the Throne there was no suggestion that the Government would deal effectively with the great question of unemployment. The paragraph in the Speech relating to that matter read:

Whilst of the opinion that unemployment relief is fundamentally a municipal and provincial responsibility, my Government has felt that as conditions have arisen in a measure out of the laite war, they would be justified in continuing for the period of the winter months the expedient of supplementing by grants from the federal treasury the relief contributions of provinces and municipalities for the purpose of alleviating actual distress.

I take it that the solution of the problem of unemployment should go a great deal further than the giving of unemployment relief, and that the problem is already of such vast importance that it cannot he dealt with satisfactorily by either provincial or municipal bodies. I have a resolution passed at the joint conference of trades unions, returned men's organizations, and representatives of other public bodies, held on February 6, 1922, at Vancouver, which embodies fairly well the position taken by a large number of unemployed people and labour organizations throughout the entire Canadian West. This resolution is as follows:

Whereas the unemployed situation is of a national character, and is one that cannot be handled satisfactorily by municipal bodies ; and whereas, the extremely low scale of relief now being given is tending to lower the standard of living of the entire wage working population; be it resolved, that we call upon the federal Government to assume the management of the unemployment situation on a national scale, and that the basis of relief be work at trade union rates or full maintenance on the scale laid down in the Labour Gazette.

In my own province of Manitoba there was held, in September, 1921, a conference on the question of unemployment. This conference was called at the invitation of the government of the province, and I have before me a series of resolutions which were drawn up at that time. It will be borne in mind that these resolutions represent the municipal and provincial aspects of the case. Among clauses dealing with the causes of unemployment I would read the following:
Fluctuations in industry are caused by market changes brought on by world conditions and social habits.
Lack of relations between system of education and the labour market, in order that the youth will be trained in occupations in which workers are in demand.

Allowing men and families to immigrate into Canada, who are not equipped, either physically or financially, to take up farm work, and who are not desirous of taking up this work, but who wish to take up other industrial activities wherein there is no demand.
The lack of organization of productive industry with a view to continuous employment.
Having laid down some of the causes of unemployment, the report proceeds with suggested measures for relief:
Undoubtedly, the unemployment problem is a national one, and must be studied from a national point of view.
I agree absolutely with the finding of the provincial conference on unemployment, that this matter cannot be dealt with satisfactorily except from a national standpoint.
Unemployment

I think this position is well taken, when we consider the action of the Peace Conference at Versailles. In the draft convention and recommendations adopted by the International Labour Conference at its first meeting in Washington during November, 1919, there occurs the following recommendation with regard to the unemployed:

As to No. 3, the minister observes that the experience of other countries has demonstrated that a system of unemployment insurance, in order to be effective and successful, must be made ancillary or complementary to a system of labour exchanges, the whole being adapted to the principal function of finding work for unemployed insured workmen. In this view, unemployed insurance has a pronounced federal aspect, and on the whole the minister thinks the establishment of a system of unemployment insurance is competent to the Dominion in the exercise of its residuary legislative powers with regard to the peace, order and good government of Canada.
Here, then, we have it admitted on the highest authority that there is a place for federal action with regard to this great question.
Now, further, may I suggest that the government has already committed itself on this question. I have a document here with this heading:

Liberals and labour. The Liberal party's record of achievement on behalf of labour, issued by the National Liberal Committee, 115 Sparks street, Ottawa. Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, M.P., Liberal leader, etc.
In this document we find the following statement:

And further resolved: (2) That insofar as may be practicable, having regard to Canada's financial position, an adequate system of insurance against unemployment, sickness, dependence in old age, and other disability, which would include old age pensions, widows' pensions, and maternity benefits, should be instituted by the federal government in conjunction with the governments of the several provinces: and that on matters pertaining to industrial and social legislation, an effort should be made to overcome any question of jurisdiction between the Dominion and the provinces by effective co-operation between the several governments.

Now, Mr. Speaker, it would seem clear from this resolution that not only is it acknowledged that the federal government has responsibilities in this matter, but also that the party in power is committed to take action along these lines.

Very little need be said here with regard to the serious situation which exists to-day. The Minister of Labour admitted in a speech, made several months ago, that there were something like 200,000 unemployed men in Canada. I presume that that would mean in the vicinity of
1,000,000 people-men, women and children

-directly affected by unemployment. That is a very, very large proportion indeed of a population of eight or nine million. I know perfectly well that in the West we have had the most serious unemployment for the last two or three years, particularly in the cities of Vancouver and Winnipeg, and to a smaller extent in nearly all the other cities, including Edmonton, Calgary and Saskatoon. And we have unemployment in the central part; I have resolutions from Toronto, Hamilton and other cities here in the East. During the recess I was down in Nova Scotia, and not only are large numbers of miners unemployed or underemployed, but there are in Sydney something like two thousand unemployed steel workers, who have absolutely no prospect of securing work in the near future and do not know where to turn to get a livelihood. It seems to me that we cannot let this session go by without taking some action to relieve the distress in which so many of our people now find themselves.

There are a few points which I should like to mention very briefly as to the position which it is necessary for us to take. There was a time in the history of Canada when, if a man were unemployed, it was his own fault. There were free lands, easily accessible, and good markets, and if a man could not succeed in one place he could go to another; and if he could not make good in one particular kind of work he could try his hand at another. That time has passed and with the system of large-scale industry that we have today a few large corporations control the greater part of the work that is available. I take that example of the steel workers at Sydney; there are several thousand of them in connection with the one great corporation there. If for any reason that corporation closes down its plant, the men are helpless. There was a time when steel working was confined to small local foundries and blacksmith shops, and in those days a man could open a little shop of his own. So far as Nova Scotia is concerned, the farms cannot absorb very many of the surplus unemployed, and they tell me there that fishing is about the only means of livelihood left, and that under present conditions it takes a considerable amount of equipment to carry on fishing successfully. A great many of the men out of work in Winnipeg are employed in railway shops and kindred work. There again I would point out that if for any reason at all the railway is not able to
Unemployment

carry on its work to the full extent, thousands of mechanics find themselves in a helpless position, for it is simply impossible for them to start up any new kind of work; they are on the street. The same thing is true in our larger mining and logging activities on the coast. I submit that to-day with large-scale industry as it is, the individual unemployed workman is not to blame. Notwithstanding that, we treat him still almost as if he were a criminal. We take it for granted almost that he is shiftless or lazy, or he would not be in such a helpless position. In any case we allow a certain maladjustment in industry to bear very heavily indeed on the unfortunate individual and his still more unfortunate family. Now, that state of affairs ought to be absolutely changed.

Another point that needs to be emphasized is that hitherto the municipalities, helped out by the provincial and Dominion governments, have been expending large sums simply for unemployment relief, and at the end of the year there is nothing to show for the expenditure. Surely, it would seem as if in Canada we had sufficient development work to do that for every hour's work there ought to be some return. This practice of putting men simply at work tests, to break stone when great crushing machines are by their side, is absolute folly. The whole trouble seems to be that we have not at the present time the necessary credit to go on with the new works we feel ought to be undertaken, and which if proceeded with would start the industrial machinery moving again. Now, there is not the slightest doubt that in this respect we are being held up, more or less, by certain interested bodies. A few weeks ago in Vancouver I was talking to an alderman who is chairman of the unemployment committee as well as of the finance committee of the council. He pointed out that much as the city would like to give some constructive work to the unemployed in Vancouver, they could not do so because they could not obtain credit from the bank-in this case, the Bank of Montreal. Upon turning to the annual statement issued by the Bank of Montreal, I find that the general manager of that institution takes .the position that unemployment is a very necessary evil; that only through unemployment can we drive down the wages to the point they should be,-or, to use the words of the report, that unemployment is a ""natural corrective."" Mr. Speaker, I think of some of the scenes which I have witnessed in

the homes of labouring men during the last few weeks: men out of work; their wives almost desperate; their children, in some instances, kept home from school through lack of shoes or clothing; in some cases not only physical privation, but absolute discouragement with regard to life itself. A large number of people are in that position; yet we are told by one of the leading financial institutions of Canada that unemployment is a ""natural corrective"". I submit that it is for the Government to defend the people of Canada against an institution of this character.

Why should we ask that the whole burden of unemployment be borne by the provinces or by the municipalities? According to our constitution, this Parliament has to deal with such great matters as immigration, fiscal policy, and so on. I submit that questions of immigration have a great deal to do with the question of unemployment. Thousands and tens of thousands of immigrants came to my own city of Winnipeg last year direct from Great Britain. Ostensibly they were to go on the land, and I believe in the first instance they did so; but the immigration officials told me at the time that there was nothing whatever to prevent these people from drifting into the city when the work of the summer was over. A number of them did drift back into the city, with the result that the municipality is loaded up with the care of them. Their presence in this country, however, is directly due to the action of this Government under its immigration policy. The same is true with regard to a good many of our large fiscal policies: we decide here what those policies shall be, but we shoulder off upon the provinces and municipalities, themselves already overloaded with debt, the responsibility of caring for the unemployed. I take it, Mr. Speaker, that we cannot do otherwise in this body than assume responsibility.

It may be said by members of the Government that it is impossible to establish a full-fledged system of unemployment insurance at this particular time. Perhaps that is a reasonable position to take, yet I would say this: until such a system can be established the least we can do is to adopt the principle underlying unemployment insurance, namely, that industry should bear the burdens entailed by industry. If we have brought more people to this country than we need, or if we have placed more people in a particular industry than we need, then the least we can do is to see that that bur-
Unemployment
den is spread out over the community, not borne by the few unfortunate individuals upon whom it now presses so heavily.

Now, without going further into this matter, I would urge that the problem is such a serious one that we should not allow many more weeks to pass before taking definite action. You may say that the spring is opening up, and that with the spring there comes agricultural work and more activity in various lines. That may be true, but we are going to have another winter, and there is no prospect that the next winter will be any better than the one which has just passed. If we are to have effective action, therefore, it must be taken at this session of Parliament. I hope hon. members will realize that while we in this House deal very largely merely with statistics and general principles, there are loyal Canadian men and women in every one of our cities to-day who are in almost desperate straits. I take it that our administrative bodies exist in order to provide for the primary needs of the people. I have said to labour audiences, and I venture to repeat it in this House, that any administrative body, in a country capable of producing as Canada can produce, which fails to provide for the primary needs of its people, even to the extent of food and clothing and shelter, ceases to command the loyalty of those people. On all sides the people in this country are calling upon us for relief, and we face a serious situation if we do not lend an ear at this time and do our utmost to solve what is not only a national but a world problem.

,Labour,,James Shaver Woodsworth,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ee1cc492-9867-48d3-a612-c1fb491d2916&Language=E&Section=ALL

,Liberal,,William Lyon Mackenzie King,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5&Language=E&Section=ALL
625290,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.9.3,1922-04-24,ee1cc492-9867-48d3-a612-c1fb491d2916,ca.m.1883,Mr. WOODSWORTH:,,THE UNEMPLOYMENT SITUATION,,,My concrete suggestion would be that at this session the Government should go into the matter and establish a system of unemployment insurance. Not that such a system would provide work, but it would give immediate and definite relief to those who are out of work, and in the effort to provide for their immediate needs we would find ourselves driven to do something along constructive lines. Most decidedly there are a number of things that could be done. Almost all our unemployment conferences have suggested lines of work which could be pursued. For example, there is a shortage of houses all

over Canada; in all our cities rentals are very high, and there is no reason why a great many more houses should not be built. On the western coast there are large areas of land which still have to be cleared; why should men be going around the cities idle when they might be engaged in the clearing of those lands? As I have said, large numbers of people lack the prime necessities of life, even of clothes; we have factories and mills standing idle which are capable of producing these things, and if these various industrial organizations cannot carry on, I do not see why the Government should not do so, and under those circumstances, put these idle men at work and see that the needs of the people are provided for. Down in Cape Breton some of the coal miners are recognizing that principle; they say that if these great corporations, some of whom have leases from the provincial government, can not see their way to make dividends and carry on, then the Government itself should step in and operate the industry in the interests of the people. There is not much doubt that there is work to do. I would venture to repeat to the Prime Minister what I said, I think, in the debate on the Speech from the Throne, that there were three factors, and three factors only, necessary in order to enable us to produce all that we require for the material welfare of the people of Canada, and those are, the natural resources of the country, the equipment and labour. I submit that we have all these three at the present time in Canada. We have natural resources in abundance. At all our Canadian Clubs we have been told of the vast extent of our natural resources. We have the equipment: factories are idle, mills and railways are not working to capacity; we have an abundance of equipment already in this country. One trouble, it seems to me, is that we have been so long adding equipment that the only possible thing we can conceive of now is to add still more equipment. We already have equipment enough; and we have labour idle. What seems to be lacking is a certain courage, and imagination that would enable us to bring these three factors into effective working connection. I cannot see why we should allow things to drift from bad to worse until some of the labour people are driven to desperation. Surely we have the brains and ability here in this House to devise some method for giving the unemployed work. If not the poor individual workman is himself surely helpless.

MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,THE UNEMPLOYMENT SITUATION,,,Let me say at the outset that I am in entire sympathy with my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woods-worth) in his desire to find some means of helping to solve the problem of unemployment where it exists. I agree with him, too, in believing that the problem of unemployment has a national significance, as well as a provincial and a municipal significance; but I think it is all important that this Parliament should very carefully consider whether the obligation of looking after men who are unemployed should become a federal obligation, rather than it should be understood to be primarily a matter for individuals in the first instance, between municipalities and the people living within their bounds, in the second instance, next, between the provinces and the citizens of the respective provinces, and only finally a matter of concern in the federal arena.

If it were admitted for one moment that it was not primarily a municipal obligation to look after the individuals who are unemployed within their bounds where would we ultimately land in the solution of this question? Should the resolution pass in the form in which I understand my hon. friend to wish it to pass, namely, as meaning that the obligation is upon the federal government to look after the unemployed, every municipality that had unemployed would immediately send its communications to Ottawa and say: The Ottawa Government, in view of the resolution that has passed this House, is obligated to look after the unemployed in this area.

625293,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.9.6,1922-04-24,b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5,ca.m.7719,Mr. MACKENZIE KING:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,THE UNEMPLOYMENT SITUATION,,,What I want to make perfectly clear is this: I do not think the Government can admit that it is primarily a federal obligation to look after the unemployed. I think that there is a national significance to the problem of unemployed, but the problem primarily is one which concerns municipalities, and secondarily, the provinces affected. It only becomes a federal problem when both the municipalities and the provinces have found it impossible to cope with a situation that is completely beyond their control. That condition has arisen, to a certain extent, as a consequence of conditions growing out

of the war, and the federal government has recognized its obligation there by promising to co-operate with the municipalities and with the provinces in the relief of their unemployed. There is a standing offer at the present time to the 4 p.m. municipalities and the provinces -a policy that was adopted by the late government, and one which has been followed by the present administration -to help them meet cases of distress where they are unable to look after their own unemployed. I am told by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) that from two or three, possibly four of the provinces of this Dominion, no request has come to the federal government for assistance. Does my hon. friend think, that the provinces which have made no request for assistance in helping to solve the unemployment problem within their boundaries would be agreeable to being taxed to assist other provinces in the matter of their unemployment as a national obligation? I am afraid that if we began to work out the question on a basis of that kind, we would find it impossible in any way to carry out such a policy. I believe with my hon. friend, as I said at the outset, that the matter is one in which there is a national interest, as well as provincial and municipal interest, but that it can only be met by co-operation between the provinces and the federal government.

The hon. member has suggested that the step that should be taken at once is for this Parliament to pass an enactment in the nature of unemployment insurance. I question very much whether, if we attempted to pass such legislation at the present time, we would find that it comes wholly within the jurisdiction of this federal Parliament. The provinces may have the right to pass such a law; we may have the right to pass such a law; but one thing is certain, that between the two of us we ought to be able to find a way to pass such an enactment if it is in the public interest. It is in that spirit that the Liberal party adopted as one of the planks in its platform the resolution which my hon. friend has quoted, and which I shall quote now, and which, let me say, expresses the policy of the Government on this question:

That in so tar as may be practicable, having regard for Canada's financial position, an adequate system of insurance against unemployment, sickness, dependence in old age, and other disability, which would include old age pensions, widows' pensions, and maternity benefits, should be instituted by the federal Government in conjunction with the Governments of
Unemployment

the several Provinces; and that on matters pertaining to Industrial and Social legislation an effort should be made to overcome any question of jurisdiction between the Dominion and the Provinces by effective co-operation between the several Governments.

That policy is one which recognizes the obligations of t)he federal government to cooperate with the provincial governments in working out a system of insurance against unemployment. That is an entirely different attitude, however, from the federal Government's admitting that the obligation is upon it to solve this question independently altogether of the municipalities and the provinces.

I would say to my hon. friend and to the House that the Minister of Labour and myself, have already been in communication with representatives of some of the provincial governments with a view to having a conference on this very subject during the course of the present year, and I think before the year is out that conference will take place; but I would like to make it perfectly plain that so far as the Government is concerned, we regard all these matters of unemployment and the like as questions primarily of concern to municipalities and to provinces, but in so far as the national interest may also be concerned we are prepared to co-operate with the municipalities and the provinces in seeking a solution.

625294,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.9.7,1922-04-24,4f144b8d-0f62-4502-b6eb-6bf2aa0faaad,ca.m.1477,Hon. R. J. MANION (Fort William and Rainy River):,,THE UNEMPLOYMENT SITUATION,,,I shall take up the time

of the House only for a few moments in any remarks I have to make on this question. There is no doubt that this is a very important question from the standpoint of any country in the world. I believe that any man who looks at this question in a fair light must decide that no class of men should be permitted to be without work and to go hungry.

We have, unfortunately, in most countries of the world been in the habit of taking better care of our animals-that is the lower animals-than, perhaps, of human animals, and I believe that, from that standpoint, the question my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) has brought up is one of importance. There is no doubt every hon. member of the House desires to see some solution, if at all possible, of the unemployment situation, which exists not only in Canada, but unfortunately is world-wide at the present time. My hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg mentioned unemployment insurance. He has been more of a student of affairs of this

kind than I have, and I presume he knows much better than I do that that type of insurance has been tried out in various parts of the world, and I think probably he knows the conclusion that I draw from my reading, namely that it has not been altogether a success. It has been tried out in a number of different countries, in various cities in Germany, in a number of cities in France, in some cities in Italy, and various other cities, and I believe in some countries almost as a whole. But there has been a great deal of abuse of this system of insurance in the different countries of the world. It has not been found an unmixed good. However, I personally wish to express my entire sympathy, as the leader of the Government (Mr. Mackenzie King) did, with the problem, but before any system of unemployment insurance could be adopted, I think it would be desirable to go into the question much more thoroughly than this House has ever done since I have been a member of it.

My hon. friend, the Prime Minister, pointed out that the Government of to-day is carrying on the programme as outlined by the government which went out of office in December, 1921. I have noticed that this pledge of the Liberal platform which he read must go into the discard, with a number of other pledges which were in the Liberal platform before the election, and I am pleased to hear the leader of the Government to-day commend what was condemned so vociferously before the election by a number of the members of the present Government. It is certainly gratifying to us on this side of the House, and it should certainly prove to the people of this country that a cure in office is a good deal more difficult than condemnation out of office.

JAMES MURDOCK (Minister of Labour) :,Minister of Labour,THE UNEMPLOYMENT SITUATION,,,I want to first state, Mr. Speaker, that I am altogether sympathetic with what I believe to be the views of my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg, in so far as we can, in an appropriate way, co-operate in dealing with this very important question of unemployment. But I fear that my hon. friend is undertaking to place an undue burden upon this federal government when he proposes to hold this Government alone responsible for dealing with the question of unemployment. My hon. friend referred
Unemployment

to certain communications on this question received by him from Vancouver. I have received some fourteen or more communications as the result of a meeting held in Vancouver on 6th February last, indicating that it was the view of an unemployed conference there that the federal government should assume charge over the conditions of unemployment, to the extent of obtaining full wages, at trades union rates, for all persons in Vancouver who were not at that time employed. I must firmly take the position that I do not see how this federal government could assume any such obligation as that, because it would be adopting a plan that might not be in the best interests of the unemployed in Canada, and would certainly place a burden upon this Dominion which would indeed be hard to carry. 625297,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.9.10,1922-04-24,3e57b464-66c8-4a1c-bf6b-c0e2e08ef1bf,ca.m.2136,Mr. MURDOCK:,Minister of Labour,THE UNEMPLOYMENT SITUATION,,,Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Quebec have generally indicated that they were amply sufficient unto themselves to deal with this question; and we, of course, are glad to understand that that is the position. The following sentences from the Speech of His Excellency the Governor General at the opening of Parliament in February indicate the attitude of the Dominion Government on the subject:

Unemployment, the world-wide result of the conditions to which I have referred, though less widespread in Canada than elsewhere, has received most anxious consideration. CARROLL (Cape Breton South and Richmond) :,,THE UNEMPLOYMENT SITUATION,,,Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to participate in any way in the discussion of this resolution, and I would not have said anything, were it not for the fact that the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth), who moved the resolution, made some mention of conditions in the city of Winnipeg. Conditions in that city are far from good, and the hon. member is well within the mark when he says that 2,000 steel workers in Sydney, who are anxious and willing to work, are out of employment at the present time and, I believe, are well nigh on the verge of starvation. Did I hear an hon. member say ""strikers""? They are not even able to ""strike on the job,"" because they have no job to strike on. Nova Scotia is a province which has not applied to this Government under the various Orders in Council which have been passed for the purpose of aid being

rendered by this Government to municipalities. That does not mean that there is not to-day dire want in Nova Scotia. As I have stated, there are in the city of Sydney 2,000 people who are only too anxious to work if they can get employment. They are not looking for charity, and they have not gone to the provincial government to ask for aid, because if they did that and received aid under present regulations in that province, they would become paupers and would cease to be citizens of this country. Perhaps that is one of the reasons why they have not gone to the Nova Scotia government to ask for aid under present legislation in that province.

I want to be quite frank. I have brought this matter to the attention of certain members of this Government, and I am going to interview members of the Government again, because last week I received communications from several clergymen in Sydney, wise men who brought this matter to my attention in a way in which it was not brought before, and I am bound to say that it is a most serious condition,

in a city of 27,000 people or thereabouts, to have 2,000 bread-winners walking the streets in idleness because there is no occupation for them. When I brought this matter to the attention of certain members of the Government, they did not say: ""We will not act;"" but I am bringing it to their attention to-day publicly, and I am going to interview them again. When I do so, I shall be reinforced by every private member from Nova Scotia, and I am going to draw to their attention the fact that there is a way out of this difficulty as regards the 2,000 steel workers in the city of Sydney. That is, the problem can be solved in that city without adding one dollar to the public debt of this country, because a way can be devised whereby the steel mills in the city of Sydney may be put into operation by this Government, if they see fit to have them put into operation, and for every dollar which will be spent by this Government in putting those mills into operation, this Government will receive a return in the shape of the product of those mills. If this Government are not able to use this product now, they will be able to use it in a very short time. I would not have spoken about this matter; but I felt, the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg having made reference to the situation in the city of Sydney, that my people down there, if I may say so, would think I was derelict in the duty in which
Unemployment

I feel I owe them-and which, I believe, the Government of this country owes them -if I did not speak on their behalf. My hon. friend said that there was a possibility of the steel workers of Sydney going on the farms or fishing. In the first place, that is not their occupation, and, as in any other occupation, success
requires years of service.

That is the first difficulty. The second difficulty is the fact that these 2,000 steel workers in the city of Sydney have not the means to procure the necessary equipment for fishing. It is true that it does not cost very much-between $200 and $400 being required. But this is altogether beyond these people. And in Nova Scotia these workmen could not go in for farming, even if they were adapted to this calling which they certainly are not. We are not a great farming community, and there are no farms that could be available for these men. Furthermore, there is an insurmountable obstacle in the lack of capital. In spite of all the circumstances that have conspired against them, however, these 2,000 men of whom my hon. friend has spoken have not gone to the government of Nova Scotia to seek one dollar of public charity, and I commend that indomitable, manly spirit on their part. At the same time they are, to my knowledge, in dire need to-day, many of their families facing actual starvation.

There is a way out of this unfortunate situation, and I trust that before the Government decide whether or not they will anticipate an order of steel rails for the city of Sydney they will take my word for it when I tell them that there is the direst necessity at this moment for some effective action. The problem is not only local; it is one of national concern. There is not a province in the entire Dominion, if my information is correct, where it is not necessary at the present time for some steps to be taken, either by the local authorities or by the Dominion government to provide relief; and I am one of those who believe that the federal government might be called upon to render more assistance to the people of the country than has been given, either by past governments or, so far, by this Government. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) has stated that $102,000 has been spent in the last two or three months in the city of Vancouver. I can tell him that in order to provide adequate relief in the present situation in Sydney, not $100,000 or $200,000, but $500,000 is necessary. What is $10,000 or $50,-

000 when distributed among 2,000 families? It is nothing. It may tide them over for a week or so, but whatever assistance it may give is fleeting. So that the time may come, if the present condition of affairs develops as in the last two months, when the federal government will have to make greater efforts than have been made in the past to alleviate the sufferings of the people. I know for a fact that the municipalities in Nova Scotia, which are not in any very different position from those of other parts of the country, are to-day financially embarrassed. At any rate, those with which I am familiar have overdrawn their accounts at the banks and have not the wherewithal to furnish relief to those who are in need. And, what is more, I doubt very much whether the provincial government, if it were called upon, would be in a position to lend any assistance. The federal government may possibly say, ""Well, we are in the same position ourselves; we have not the funds."" Well, Sir, let there be more co-operation. Take the municipality of the county of Cape Breton, for example. The county council of Cape Breton meets once a year, in the month of January, and if any parts of the municipality were in need of relief it would take a considerable length of time to convene the council and adopt measures cooperative with the province, or with this Government, for that matter. The Order in Council which was passed some months ago offering relief to soldiers embraced only certain classes of men, those who were getting pensions and those who were receiving vocational training, and it therefore did not meet the requirements of the municipalities, and the various districts generally, in the province from which I come.

Now, sir, I wish to inform this House that the people of the province of Nova Scotia are neither thriftless nor lazy, but are desirous, nay more, anxious, to work. They are not a class who would evade the responsibility which they owe their families, their friends, or the public at large. The labouring classes in that province, I say, are anxious and eager to get employment that they may earn a livelihood, because they have not looked for charity and are not doing so now. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, many of them would starve rather than go looking for charity. I hope, therefore, that the Government will believe me when I repeat that there is the most urgent necessity for some effective action in the city of Sydney and its vicinity. In regard to the
Unemployment

miners, there is the question of wages; and I do not think my hon. friend from Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) will say that at the present time there is any large amount of unemployment in the coal industry in Nova Scotia. The question of wages is entirely another matter, and I hope that in a very short time the question will be settled when it comes before the conciliation board, which is now being reconvened. At this particular stage, where promptness of action is imperative, I do not think that an investigation into the matter of insurance against unemployment is going to help the situation. No investigations of any kind will relieve the distress that exists; immediate action is necessary. When, however, the question of insurance against unemployment, the question of old age pensions, and other social questions which have been more or less engaging the public mind for some time, are brought to the forefront, I can assure my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg that they will find a staunch supporter and an ardent friend in myself.

625304,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.9.17,1922-04-24,intervention,,,,THE UNEMPLOYMENT SITUATION,,,I think the Government ought to be able, as the motion reads, to determine its
column2: meaning and to

column1: decide its position with regard thereto. For myself,
column2: I do not want

column1: to be understood as voting in any atmosphere of doubt when I record my judgment
on this resolution. I have no trouble whatever in determining my position.

The resolution implies that in so far as relief is concerned the principle we have followed is inadequate and does not get us far enough, and that some new principle, some new scheme should be sought out and adopted, placing upon the federal authorities the initial and primary burden for relief from distress. So far as that is concerned, whether as leader of the Government, or as leader of the Opposition, or as a private member, I have no doubt as to where I ought to stand-none whatever.

I agree wholly with the principle that when it comes to the handing out of relief to those in want and distress, the obligation is primarily municipal; if it passes the municipality, the next obligation is on the province; and lastly, and only lastly, on the federal authority. I believe that if we depart from the principle of primary municipal responsibility, we land ourselves in a Serbonian bog from which we will not emerge, and this House should not countenance departing from that principle for any reason whatsoever. Consequently I oppose the resolution.

I oppose it because I believe it seeks to put this House on a false basis with regard to unemployment relief. I do not for a moment say that we have no responsibility with regard to unemployment; not at all. The primary duty of the federal parliament is to adopt such measures of high public policy as will bring to a minimum unemployment, and spread to the utter most limits employment amongst our people.

May I compliment the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Carroll)? I know not what he has in mind in suggesting that there are things which may be done in the way of legislation which will conduce to employment among those out of work. That is something for this House to consider. If he has something practical, something which will really bring about that result, I would be disposed to favorably consider it. As I say, I do not know what he has in mind, but consideration of the subject he mentions is the primary duty of the federal parliament. When it comes to actually relieving those in distress, that is the primary duty of the municipalities and the provinces.
Now, is the Government following the proper course as regards both of these responsibilities?-first, to so dispose public
Unemployment

policy as to make employment general and remunerative, which is the initial and major responsibility?-second, to take care to the extent of its last, not initial, responsibility of such residuum of distress as may remain? As to the first, we will know better when the programme of the Government comes down. The Order Paper as yet is absurdly barren,-the most anaemic indeed that I ever have witnessed. But there are still some weeks ahead and there are those who have some hope left. Consequently the time for the discussion of that phase has not yet come. As to the second, as the Prime Minister has stated, the Government is following the principle laid down by the late administration,- the principle of placing the task of actually taking care of the unemployed upon the local authorities. Follow any other course, and what results? Not relief to the people generally, but only the encouragement of unemployment locally due to the knowledge that locally they would not have to bear the strain.

Now, there is one thing in the statement of the Prime Minister that really I do not understand. I hope that he only made a mistake. He stated there were four provinces which had not asked for assistance in the matter of relieving unemployment, and that those four provinces should not be called upon to give any assistance in the way of general relief. Let us inquire into that declaration. Under the late administration the municipalities were asked to put in the machinery to provide relief, where relief could not be avoided and was called for by all the claims of mercy and decency, and then to call on the provincial authorities to provide one-third of the actual disbursements,-not of the disbursements for the machinery at all; we did not propose that we or the provinces pay any of the expenses of organization-but only one-third of the actual amount that reached the unemployed. If the province and the municipality did so we would pay a third. That placed upon the general federal taxpayer the obligation to pay one-third of the residuum of actual relief.

We went further. We said1: In so far as the disabled returned soldier is concerned, he is the special charge of the Government. He has suffered in the war, and it may be that because of his suffering he particularly comes in contact with the distress incident to unemployment because often he is the first to be discharged. Therefore, as respects the disabled returned man, we

said we could and did take care of him altogether. That is the extent to which we went, and I think we spent something over one million dollars last year in taking care specially of these disabled returned men. I do not know just what the expenditure was in the general relief, one-third of which we bore.

,,,Right Hon ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):,

,Liberal,,William Lyon Mackenzie King,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5&Language=E&Section=ALL
625306,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.9.19,1922-04-24,d02a7b53-dad0-4944-82b0-aed9054a7bc2,ca.m.4870,Mr. MEIGHEN:,Leader of the Official Opposition,THE UNEMPLOYMENT SITUATION,,,What the Prime Minister said was: Would it be fair to expect these four provinces, which were not asking for anything themselves, to contribute to the relief of unemployment in the other provinces. He said it would not be fair. Whether he referred to the present method or any method is perfectly immaterial. If it is a false principle to call upon a province which does not ask for relief itself to contribute to unemployment relief in another province that does ask it, then that applies to anything which invokes that principle. In other words, if you use a principle that is false, you are doing wrong. Let me repeat. If it is wrong to call upon a province that itself takes care of its own obligations to assist a province that does not, then that is a good principle and you should not invade it. You invade it by the system now in vogue. Consequently I say it is either not a good principle or we should depart from the system now in vogue.

I think it is not a good principle I think that you can fairly ask the whole Dominion to assist on certain conditions in the relief of unemployment. But you must not go too far, you must go only a short distance in that regard; and the reason we came to that opinion was this: The conditions which resulted from the war were such that un-
Unemployment
employment was to some extent-in what measure it was impossible exactly to say

the direct result of the war itself. Therefore, because of the returned soldier obligation we felt in justice bound to assume and spread over the whole of Canada some share of the unemployment burden. That reason seemed to me good. If I did not believe it I would have to oppose the Government's policy, and I could not justify the policy that the late government adopted.

Now, the present Government, while following precisely the principle that we applied, not departing in any way whatever from it, did alter the proportions; but instead of altering them along the line of the principle suggested by the leader of the Government to-day, it altered them exactly the opposite way. It said to the municipality: Your responsibility is primary, but the share you pay will be the least of all. We will pay half, you will pay only one-sixth, and the province one-third; that makes the whole, whereas before the municipality paid a third, the province a third and the Dominion a third. Consequently over the whole of Canada he spreads now half-more than ever-making the very provinces that asked for nothing contribute more than they ever contributed before to the relief of provinces that asked for federal help. In a word, his policy is a direct antitheses to his expression of sentiment. However,'it is not the first time that that incident has occurred.

Now, the Prime Minister, in regard to the unemployment insurance question, reads from the Liberal platform. You will be delighted, Mr. Speaker, and we all are, to hear at last a reference to the Liberal platform from the lips of the Prime Minister. I am sure all are in accord with me when I say that this is the first time that platform has been brought into the realm of this House since he reached his present exalted post; this is the first time he has read from its provisions. But, may I ask, Mr. Speaker, what is this resolution that he says his Government actually binds itself to fulfil? It is a pretty safe resolution. He says that if it is in the public interest-these are words that my hon. friend placed in it as he read-and if the public finances will permit, and when they permit, and if it is within our powers, then we ought to find some way of co-operating with the provinces in order to introduce unemployment insurance. If one can improve on that for a resolution that by a circuitous excursion finally ends
[Mr. Meighen.1

by saying nothing, that at least he has exceeded my powers of circumlocution. The Prime Minister having seized on this lone declaration of the Liberal platform and declared his fidelity to it, I conclude that the plan of the Government is this: only to give heed to the programme of the Liberal convention when the resolution in question is surrounded at all four points of the compass with a wide-open ""if"" and when there is nothing but swinging doors in between.

MACLEAN (South York):,,THE UNEMPLOYMENT SITUATION,,,Mr. Speaker, just for a moment I would like to bring to the attention of the House the condition of affairs in our own province of Ontario, where a certain dispute has arisen between the Hydro-Electric Commission and the provincial government. 625308,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.9.21,1922-04-24,f0d1049a-4acc-4789-a93f-b3bceae69e3f,ca.m.8624,Mr. WILLIAM IRVINE (East Calgary) :,,THE UNEMPLOYMENT SITUATION,,,Mr. Speaker, it is very interesting to note that all hon. members who have spoken on this question agree as to its importance and its urgency. I want to make a few practical suggestions, seeing that hon. members on the Government side have not made any, and that the hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) has not made any. It has been stated that the member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) has not made any. So perhaps I may be pardoned if I attempt at least to make one or two. If the suggestions I make are not of any value, we simply ask that the
Unemployment
Government take this matter into consideration and themselves make suggestions that will be of value.

There is no idea on our part to charge the present employment situation to this Government. We understand that they have no more to do with it than we have. We are simply urging that it is a question of national importance, and that, therefore, it is a question that cannot be passed by as merely something for the municipalities or for the provinces. Those who have been connected with labour for some years know that the municipalities take precisely the same attitude -that this Government has taken. They say: ""This is not a matter for us; we have no authority."" And the provincial governments say the very same thing. But when we come to this House we find the federal government saying that the municipalities or the provinces are responsible. I think it is reasonable to suggest -that the Government should in the first place find out who is responsible. It would be well for labour, it would be well for the members of this House and of other legislative bodies, to know who has authority in these matters. The question seems at present to be undecided, for both the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the leader of the Opposition-for once in the same camp-have stated very definitely that this is a matter for the municipalities and must not be taken out of their hands. I am not suggesting that it should be taken out of their hands, but I want to know whether it is actually in their hands now. It seems to me that matters of unemployment or anything else pertaining to labour are pretty much of a football that is kicked around from one authority to the other. It is necessary that we should know where the authority lies.

Now, the unemployment situation is not a new thing, nor is it going to be settled permanently with the coming of summer; it is a problem that has arisen out of the economic system that prevails. I do not think, nor do I believe that the other representative of labour thinks, that the question can be ultimately settled in this House. But we do think that something of a practical nature can be put forward. The Prime Minister challenged the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg to offer a practical suggestion. That is only fair, but I would like to remipd the Prime Minister that he already has had a very practical suggestion from the organized labour movement of Canada: I refer to the case as presented to his Government by the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada. The Trades and Labour Congress have put forward a solution which seems to them to be good; it is the only one, or the best one, they have been able to think of. As I say, it has been placed in the hands of the Government. I do not know what the Government are going to do with it, but I want to put upon Hansard what the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada request of the Government with regard to unemployment:
We recommend the enactment ot unemployment insurance embodying the following principles t-

column2: Creation of a federal fund, from which payments may be made to unemployed, and under employed persons.
This fund to be raise-d by assessment on the pay rolls of undertakings whose workers are covered by such insurance and added to by Dominion and, if possible, provincial public funds.
Payments to be made to workers during actual unemployment or when employed for fixed periods for less than 75 per cent of thedr regular working hours.
No employer to be allowed to discharge numbers of his workers without due notice to the Employment Service of Canada, so as to give them an opportunity to provide for their redistribution.
The Government to have power to investigate as to the real need of discharge of workers, and consequent limitation of production.
No employers to be allowed to discharge workers for lack of work, until the hours of such industry have been reduced to at least half of the normal working hours.
Workers in this way underemployed to have their wages supplemented from the federal fund up to not less than 75 per cent of their normal earnings.
This Act to apply -to workers under pub-lie bodies as well as to private employers.

Use of the advisory councils of the employment services should be made for the carry-mg out of the act, and power given them to deal with matters relating to the co-ordinating of public works, and perhaps their partial financing from the fund, in order to avoid unemployment. These suggestions are by no means complete but would provide a starting point for this much needed legislation.

column1: That is the starting point which the organized labour movement of Canada has suggested to this Government, and I repeat, if that is not considered to be a feasible proposition, let the Government provide a more feasible one. Inasmuch as they have admitted that this is a question of grave importance which they are willing to see settled, have they a better solution than the one suggested, and if so, what is it? I think the Labour representatives in this House will be only too glad to suprevised EDITION

port the Government if they have a solution that they consider better than the one I have just mentioned.

I want to offer another suggestion. If unemployment insurance is not considered to be practicable at the present time, and if the Government has no other substitute proposal, I want to read just a clause from the proposal put forward by the Trades and Labour Council of Calgary. This is merely a palliative, as they call it, but it might be worthy of consideration. I simply offer it to the Government at its face value:

That the Dominion, provincial governments and municipalities prepare estimates for all public works that can he possibly carried out during the winter months, and that tenders for same be prepared and submitted early in the fall to eliminate any unnecessary waiting to start the work when needed.
That the Dominion Government take under consideration the further construction of the national highways with a view that same be eventually completed from coast to coast.
These are the two principal palliatives.
I do not know whether the Government will adopt them, but at all events I have submitted them for consideration.

In conclusion, the Government has already committed itself on this question. It has already paid out doles to the unemployed in Canada. It has accepted partial responsibility, at least, in conjunction with provincial and municipal governments for aiding the unemployed. That is an assumption at least of partial responsibility. Furthermore, the Government, I understand, has assumed responsibilities for losses which may have been incurred by large corporations who were engaged in producing munitions and other war material. If I am not mistaken, the British Empire Steel Corporation in Nova Scotia actually received subsidies-perhaps that is not the exact term-because when the war ceased they were left with a great plant on their hands and seemingly could not make anticipated profits. The Government, I understand, reimbursed them to the extent of their probable losses. Surely, if the Government can undertake to reimburse a company for probable losses, it ought to assume some responsibility for the men who are thrown out of work by 5 p.m. that company. That is not asking too much; in my opinion, it is a reasonable proposition. I believe that the Government is just as sincere in trying to solve the unemployment problem as I am, and I have no hesitation in saying so. I believe that the leader of the Opposition

(Mr. Meighen) is also sincere. But it seems that while we all think it is a great and serious problem which we would all wish to see partially or completely solved, nobody seems to know what to do about it. Does that mean that we must drop the matter there, bury it and leave it; that we will not continue to make a study of this question? Would it not be possible for the Government to have a Standing Committee appointed to study this question and continue to make proposals? Because I can assure the House that unemployment is going to be with us much longer than this summer. Next winter is likely to be as bad if not worse than the last, and now is the time to take precautionary measures and do everything possible to prevent unemployment being as prevalent throughout Canada as it was last winter. If the suggestions put forward by the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada are not practicable, and if the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) and myself have not contributed anything of value, let not the effort stop there; let us find some body who can give us something of value.

I have another suggestion, and it is that this Government take steps towards calling a national conference at which municipal and provincial governments and the Dominion Government will be represented, for the purpose of taking into consideration the proposals of the Peace Conference and seeing what action shall be taken regarding them.

625309,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.9.22,1922-04-24,ee1cc492-9867-48d3-a612-c1fb491d2916,ca.m.1883,Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Centre Winnipeg) :,,THE UNEMPLOYMENT SITUATION,,,First, one or two remarks on the suggestions that have been put forward in this discussion by hon. members who have spoken.

It was suggested by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock), I think, that a certain number of the unemployed in Vancouver were there because they were unwilling to go out on the prairies. A great many of them last spring did go out on the prairies, but were sent back because there was no work for them to do. There were advertisements, I believe, placed in some of the papers on the prairies protesting against any more men being brought over the mountains from the West. Then, as is very well known, owing to the seasonal character of agriculture, after the thresh-
Unemployment

ing is over on the prairies large numbers of men have no further work to do on the farms; that is, there are more men needed on the farms just at threshing time than during the winter months, and those unemployed drift back into the cities, and, of course, a considerable number of them drift back over the mountains to Vancouver. But this situation is no fault of the men who are found out of work during the winter time. It arises as I said before because of certain mal-adjustments in our industrial system itself.

Again, we are told that charity ought to begin at home, and that the municipalities ought to take action in this matter. A very large number of municipalities, at least in the West, have taken action in this matter, and it is only after they have found themselves unable to cope with the situation that they have referred the matter to the provincial governments. In turn, it is only after the provincial governments have found that the question was altogether too big for them, that the federal government has been appealed to. In the resolution of the conference called by the Manitoba Government, which I read it was distinctly urged that the problem was on such a large scale that it could not be solved short of being treated as a national problem.

One hon. gentleman from the East suggested that I had thought that possibly the steel workers might go fishing. He did not catch my point at all. I stated that some people had suggested: Why not go into other classes of work?-why should they not go fishing? And my position was precisely that which the hon. member took, that it would be impossible for them to go fishing or engage in any other occupation which required considerable equipment.

I have no great hope that the problem of unemployment will be solved simply by introducing a policy of unemployment insurance. I frankly admit that unemployment insurance has not been a full success in places where it has been tried. But it has accomplished something. We are faced with a world condition today. Some believe that our economic problems can be solved only by the most radical and far-reaching changes in our whole economic system. I am one of those. But I may be mistaken. If the present system of organization is capable of carrying on, give it a chance. If it is capable of providing for the wants of the people, give it every opportunity, but, in the meantime, do not let us permit the men and G9i

women, and especially the little children to suffer. If the existing system can take care of the people, that may show that some of us are wrong when, as we try to analyse the situation, we conclude that other and more radical changes are necessary. Some of us have been fairly closely associated with what is known as radical labour throughout western Canada and I should like this House to know there is a very strong impression among quite large groups of labour that it is next to impossible to accomplish anything through the action of Parliamment. They have almost given up hope. Some of us have stated that we ought to use parliamentary power to the full extent. Others reply that such a course would be useless. Really I do not know but that they are right. If we come here asking for so simple a thing as that this Government should undertake measures to provide for the men that are confessedly on the verge of starvation, and who have had to be fed by the municipalities during the winter months, and if this Government refuses to take action to provide, even for primary needs of that kind, I am sure it gives force to the contention it is hopeless to secure any reforms of far-reaching character through our parliamentary machinery. The Prime Minister speaks of being willing to co-operate with the provinces and municipalities. ""Co-operate"" is a good word, but I would like to have a little bit more definiteness in regard to it. There has been up to the present co-operation in the giving of relief. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) says the way is still open for cooperation in the giving of more relief. My resolution looks to some action more far-reaching than the simple giving of doles. It looks at least in the direction of a permanent solution of this problem, or, if not a permanent solution, then more adequate care for the people who at present are being crushed under our present system. The Prime Minister says he would be quite favourable to the resolution if it were understood that it does not mean that the federal government assumes exclusive jurisdiction in this matter, and that it does not mean that it would take responsibility from the provinces or municipalities. I have no desire, whatever, to remove responsibility from the provinces or municipalities. I have, as a matter of fact, very little interest in these purely jurisdictional affairs. I want to secure definite construction action. If the Premier can assure us that the Government
Unemployment
will go forward in the near future and give us some definite action that is all that any of us require at this particular time. My resolution reads:
That in the opinion of this House, in view of the widespread unemployment with which the municipalities and provinces find themselves unable to cope-*
That is, I think substantiated by the resolutions which have come forward to the Government, copies of which resolutions have been furnished to all of us.
-it is desirable that the federal Government should devise some means of dealing effectively with the situation.

That is intended to place upon the Government the responsibility of finding the best means of meeting the situation. In this resolution we are not even urging unemployment insurance. That is thrown out merely as a constructive suggestion. We are urging upon the Government definite action, so that the people who are now suffering shall not have to go through another winter such as that through which they have just passed.
