625317,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.11.4,1922-04-24,deaf5a4f-d8a1-49b8-a81b-f90eeaf06463,ca.m.9018,Mr. ANDREW McMASTER (Brome) :,,MINISTERS AND DIRECTORSHIPS,,,I ask the attention of hon. members of this House to what this motion proposes to do, and what it proposes not to do. It does not propose that members of the Government who are directors in companies carrying on what I might call private businesses should resign their directorships. If a member is carrying on the business, let us say, of a wholesale grocer in corporate form, I do not propose that he should, on becoming a member of the Cabinet, resign his directorship in such company. I propose that his company should be put exactly in the same position as if it were owned by him in non-corporate form, and that the company should not have the privilege of doing any business with the Government. What I claim for this resolution is that it proposes to prevent a possible conflict of fiduciary interests and that it is framed for the purpose of asking the opinion of this House as to the undesirability of members of the Government being at the same time directors in great public corporations, such as the banks, trust companies, transportation companies and great public utility corporations. I trust that I shall be able to place before the House such arguments as will lead it to the belief that what I am endeavouring to do now is in the public interest. I may say, what I said in introducing this matter last year, that I desire to discuss it on the plane of principle and not on that of personality; that I attack, not an individual, but a practice.

This is not the first time that I have brought such matters before the House. Last session, I introduced a bill providing that within fifteen days of accepting office, all ministers of the Crown who were directors in companies-and at that time I made no differentiation between large companies and small companies-should resign their directorships. I have changed that attitude; this session I have not gone so far as I did last year. I have not gone so far, largely because arguments were advanced last year which showed me that it was unwise to go so far as I went on that occasion. What were the arguments used against my bill last year? There was, first of all, the argument that it was unwise, improper. I will deal with that criticism
Ministers and Directorships

in a moment. There were other criticisms; there was the criticism that the bill went too far in that it tried to crystallize into legislation what should be rather left to the feelings of ministers themselves. There was also the argument that it went too far; that it was unfair to ask a man who was say, carrying on a business individual to himself, in corporate form, to resign a directorship in such business. I have met those two last criticisms. I am not asking for legislation on this occasion; I am not asking that men who are carrying on their private business or their partnership business in corporate form should, on assuming office, have to resign their directorships in such companies. But I am returning to the charge in respect of the holding of directorships in banks, trust companies and transportation companies, and the first point that I wish to make is that everything which has happened in this country in respect of the holding, by ministers of the Crown, of directorships in banks, trust companies and such other organizations since the introduction of my bill of last year, has ratified, confirmed and approved everything that I said in that connection on that occasion.

I do not wish to delay the House unduly with this matter, for it seems to me that what I have to say is of primordial, primary soundness. I think I shall have the general agreement of hon. gentlemen who sit on both the front benches of this House, when I say that, in this country, the life of a minister is one of unremitting toil. Our practice in this country imposes upon ministers vast amounts of routine business, and it is only with difficulty that a minister is able to obtain the time required to study policies. I say that we have the very best of authority that no man can serve two masters. There is nothing that one can do better in connection with such a matter as this than to give an example. There is no stronger argument, I humbly submit, as to the soundness of the position which I am assuming on this occasion, then what happened in connection with the Merchants Bank of Canada. On the 31st of November last, the Merchants Bank of Canada possessed, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, some hundreds of branches. It claimed to have a capital stock of about $10,500,000 and a reserve of about $9,000,000. For some months prior to the 7th day of December, it had been paying to its shareholders, by way of bonus or dividends, a

profit at the rate of about 13 per cent. On the latter date the people of Canada were astounded to learn that the bank was in a very bad way. It was reported that the reserve had been practically wiped out. It was found that great losses had occurred through advances to a stock-broking firm and also to a manufacturing concern of which a representative of the bank had been in charge, or in charge, to a certain extent, of the finances for many months. That was the situation which confronted the Canadian people on that occasion.

The ex-Minister of Marine and Fisheries was a director of the Merchants Bank of Canada. The Merchants Bank of Canada, as the House knows, was sold out to the Bank of Montreal. I make no complaint of the sale; it may have been the very best thing that could have happened, in view of the situation in which that bank found itself on the 7th of December, 1921. But the minister in question was also a director of the Royal Trust Company, which is considered to be and which is, I think, in fact the side-door of the Bank of Montreal, and it is a matter, difficult for any outsider to the transaction, to state whether, in this transaction, the minister in question represented the interests of the Merchants Bank of Canada, which was the vendor, or the interests of the Bank of Montreal, which Was the vendee, or the general interests of the Canadian people. I am charging no wrongdoing against any one; but I say that it is an unwholesome position for a man to find himself in, that people cannot tell which side of the bargain he is supposed to be looking after. To my proposed legislation of last year, the then Minister of Marine and Fisheries was an outspoken opponent. Although, when I address the House, I seldom weary it by reading extracts, may I be allowed to read a little of the debate which took place last year in connection with this matter? The Minister of Marine and Fisheries in the last administration said:

I have no hesitation in stating that I am a director of banks and trust companies. I ask how could it be otherwise? A man who enters business early in life, achieves a success, and becomes associated not only with a large industrial concern-of which he may happen to be the president, vice-president or managing director-but with other commercial undertakings in the city or town in which he resides, and who amasses wealth, will find himself invited to become a director of other large corporations, banks or trust companies. If a man is not successful in business, and if he is not possessed of good Judgment he will not find himself on any of these various directorates.
Ministers and Directorships

Now, suppose a business man is called to serve bis country? It is a well-known fact that business men have no desire to become members of Parliament, great as the honour is, or to become members of a government, although they appreciate to the full what that honour means. Judging from the political history of Canada and other countries it is a rare thing to find a business man, who has succeeded in commerce or in finance, either a member of the (popular chamber or a member of any particular Cabinet. But, Sir, if the State does call that man, there is only one thing for him to do. He must place the duties of his public office, the duty of serving his country, before his business interests, and henceforward devote all his time and all his attention to the administration of those public affairs to which he has been called. If I may be permitted to make a personal reference for a moment my position as a member of the Government and a member of the House is no different from the position which would be taken by any other business man. I had, of course, to drop all my business connections as far as giving them any personal attention was -concerned; I have not been able to attend to the duties of the various boards to which I belong. But, Mr. Speaker, is At fair for the hon. member (Mr. MeMaster) to expect a business man identified with large interests in this country to at once resign from those boards upon his entering the Government ?
In closing the debate, I made this reply to the Hon. Mr. Ballantyne:

Now, I come to the argument made by the Minister of Marine (Mr. Ballantyne). I may say-and I would call all members of this House to witness who heard me the other day -that in introducing this measure I studiously refrained from imputing any wrong-doing to any minister, and I refrained absolutely from making a personal attack upon any one. But the Minister of Marine has endeavoured to attract the lightning upon himself; his doing so has been no fault of mine. The minister has been frank, if he has been anything. He said: I am a director in many large industrial companies, in banks and in trust companies. He seems to think that his holding of these positions is perfectly compatible with his being a minister of the Crown,-and he now nods his head in token of assent. But, Mr. Speaker, he goes on to say this: The energy and the skill required in the administration of a large department of the Government is such that I have not been able to give any attention to my company matters; -and he nods his head again. Well, in all kindness I ask him, is it fair to the shareholders of the Royal Trust Company that he should remain a director of that company, that he should give his name to the institution and the prestige that his name carries with it, while he gives no attention at all to the affairs of the Company? Is it fair, is it right, for a man to hold himself out as a guardian of the interests of the shareholders and of the depositors, if there are any, of the Royal Trust Company, and yet give no attention to the affairs of the Company? My hon. friend is a director, if I mistake not-and he will correct me if I make any mistake-of the Merchants Bank of Canada. Is it fair or right that the working men of this country should be invited to place their hard-earned savings in the care of the Merchants Bank of Canada, relying upon my hon. friend being a director of that institution, when as a matter of fact he tells us that he can give no attention
to the matter? I do not think it is right, and I think that on further consideraition, my hon. friend will come to the same conclusion.

I think, Mr. Speaker, that the people of Canada who have seen what (happened in connection with this bank have come to the conclusion which the member for Brome formed last session in respect of this matter. I need not stress this point. But for a minister of the Crown to hold positions in which he is a trustee for other people's money, when the work entailed in his office as minister precludes him from giving any attention to the affairs of the institution which is taking care of that money, is, I respectfully say, unfair to the minister himself, unfair to the cabinet of which he is a member, unfair to the party to which he belongs, and unfair to the people of the country of which he is supposed to be one of the governors in charge of affairs. A man comes to occupy a great position in connection with business matters if he allows his name to be used as a director. He gives notice to the world that, so far as concerns the policy of the institution in question, he takes his share of responsibility; and although he does not pretend to look after the details himself, he will see that they are properly looked after.

Now let us pass to another phase of the question. The world has been struggling for years past for political equality, for social equality, and now for economic equality. In this struggle men see, with a considerable amount of uneasiness, the fact that in this country, as in others, the money power is becoming centralized in fewer and fewer hands. That is a matter on which we might have a long and interesting discussion. Interlocking directorates tie together a large number of the great financial and industrial institutions of the country. I am not going to discuss that question to-day, but the point I shall make before the House, and perhaps in some degree before the country, is that interlocking directorates should not get past the door that guards the entrance to the executive council of the nation. A friend of mine Who is conversant with business matters has prepared a graph for me in which he^ has put, in most striking form, the connection existing between the great financial, industrial and transportation interests of this country. On one side of the page I hold in my hand there appear the names of fifteen leading men of this country who are directors in large institutions. On the other side of the page, there are the names of sixteen great financial, in-

625321,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.11.8,1922-04-24,deaf5a4f-d8a1-49b8-a81b-f90eeaf06463,ca.m.9018,Mr. McMASTER:,,MINISTERS AND DIRECTORSHIPS,,,I suppose that is a fair question. I wished, if possible, to keep companies within a certain class, and that class covered great companies which were

I can easily imagine that an argument could be made out that no director whose company was the supposed beneficiary of the protective system should have a seat in the Cabinet; but to do that I would have to shut out the directors of perhaps half of the industrial life of this country, and I thought that would be going too far. In connection with any reform it is always easy to put forward the stereotyped criticism, that it goes too far, or does not go far enough. If I have the co-operation and enthusiastic support of Leader No. 2 to this resolution I will be satisfied so far as this afternoon is concerned.

Now, the next point I wish to make is that the position I am assuming now, as I assumed last year, is in conformity with present legislation on the subject-the House of Commons and Senate Act, R.S.C., 1906, chapter 10. section 14 provides:

No person, directly or indirectly, alone or with any other, by himself or by the interposition of any trustee or third party, holding or enjoying, undertaking or executing any contract or agreement, expressed or implied, with or for the Government of Canada on behalf of the Crown, or with or for any of the officers of the Government of Canada, for which any public money is to be paid, shall be eligible as a member of the House of Commons or shall sit or vote in the said House.
And section 21 provides:

No member of the Senate or of the House of Commons shall receive or agree to receive any compensation, directly or indirectly, for services rendered, or to be rendered, either by himself or another, in relation to any bill, proceeding, contract, claim, controversy, charge, accusation, arrest or other matter before the Senate or the House of Commons, or before a committee of either House, or in order to influence or -to attempt to influence any member of either House.

I do not think the passing of such a law was any reflection upon the judiciary, any more than the introduction of his resolution is intended to be or is, if properly considered, any reflection upon the members of this or any past government. Section 33 of the Judges Act reads:

No judge of the Supreme Court of Canada or of the Exchequer Court of Canada or of any superior or county court in Canada, shall, either directly or indirectly, as director or manager of any corporation, company or firm, or in any other manner whatever, for himself or others, engage in any occupation or business other than his judicial duties; but every such judge shall devote himself exclusively to such judicial duties.
Then my resolution is in line with the provisions of the law respecting the Board of Railway Commissioners. This statute is known as the Board of Railway Com-

Of course, if they cannot be shareholders in companies making these devices, they cannot be directors in such companies; therefore my resolution is in line with that legislation concerning the Board of Railway Commissioners. The Cabinet is a court of appeal to which the findings of the Railway Commission may be taken; therefore my resolution merely asks that the personnel of that court of appeal should be subject to the same limitation as the court of first instance, the Railway Commissioners of Canada.

Then, the next point, which to me is a very important one, is that the resolution follows the best practice in Canada. I have been told, and I believe it to be a fact, that when Sir Robert Borden became Prime Minister of Canada he resigned all his directorships. I am told on the authority of the Leader of the official Opposition that the former Minister of Finance, Sir Thomas White, gave up all his directorships when he became Finance Minister of Canada. And the attitude of the members of the party sitting to your right, Mr. Speaker, is in line with my resolution. I wish it were possible for the Speaker of this House to descend upon the Floor this afternoon and give me the valuable help of his eloquent voice as he did when I introduced my bill on a former occasion. On that occasion the present Speaker said:

Some years ago this Parliament amended the Judicature Act to provide that judges who had been appointed directors and were drawing directors' fees in joint stock companies or in any other company must resign. I may be told at once that no judge was ever accused of being partial in his decisions because he was a director of a company. That may be the case, but there is a great principle involved in this matter, and it is that the public must have absolute confidence in the integrity and probity of those who administer the law. It was for that purpose-that the public might respect the more the Bench of Canada-that this Parliament decided that judges should not be directors of any company. The legislation evoked

considerable discussion at the time, and some of the judges protested against what they called this hardship fieing imposed upon them; yet public opinion ratified the action of Parliament. Every litigant approved of it because, as we say in common parlance, Caesar's wife must be above suspicion.
At the end of his interesting remarks, he said:

But I say that it is in the interests of the ministers of the Crown, and of good government and of the good reputation of Parliament, that public opinion should be satisfied that there are no conflicting interests between ministers as such and any directors of private concerns. Why, it is obvious that any day of the month a minister of the Crown who has charge of a large sipending department-let us take, for example, the Public Works Department, the Department of Marine and Fisheries, or the Department of the Interior-might be put in a very awkward position as between his fiduciary interests as member of a board and his public duties on the other hand. It may happen any day, and therefore I think, without having gone very deeply into the matter, that my Hon. friend is living up to British custom, to precedent, and tradition in advocating this legislation.

I do not believe I need go further in pointing out that when this matter came before the House last year, in the consideration of my hill, the party to which I have the honour to belong was very strongly in favour of the measure-not unanimously; there were some who did not like to go as far as I have gone. For instance, the member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) felt that my motion went too far. I have largely met his objections; therefore I can recall to his attention and to the attention of others who were in the House when I made my speech last year, these words of his:

If my hon. friend were to introduce legislation that would prevent incorporated companies that had on their directorate a Minister of the Crown from doing business with the Government, I submit that he would be upon sound ground, but I fear the measure now before the House will be misunderstood, will do no good, and will not attain the object which my hon. friend desires. I am sure he had nothing personal in his mind when he introduced this measure. I am not going to offer him advice, because he is better posted upon these questions than I am, but it does seem to me that if he wishes to create such conditions as will prevent incorporated companies from abusing their privileges he might very well introduce such a measure as will put an incorporated company, with a director in the ministry, upon the same basis as a private man doing business.
That is precisely what my resolution tries to do.

No person accepting or holding the office of first minister-

Provided, however, that the provisions of this section shall not apply to holding office of or acting as a director of any company incorporated for purely religious, charitable, philanthropic, or educational purposes.

Some of them who are before me to-night made glowing speeches on that occasion, stating in eloquent terms their reasons for supporting the drastic and sweeping proposal then put forward by the hon. member for Brome. But the hon. member who went further than any one else in that respect was my hon. friend who now occupies the high position of Prime Minister. It is true that he did not on that occasion deliver what one might call a speech upon the bill, but he interjected a few remarks that showed very very clearly what his position was in regard to it. He was prepared to go even further than the bill went; he was

prepared to out-Herod Herod-or perhaps I should say out-McMaster McMaster, if the rules of the House will permit of such an expression. If, Mr. Speaker, you will turn to page 589 of Hansard you will_ see exactly what was said by my hon. friend the Prime Minister, then the leader of the Opposition. Let me give this quotation in the language of Hansard:
Mr. Meighen:
column2: (During Mr. McMaster's

column1: Speech) : Does the hon. member not think that if his bill is to be accepted it should, under our present practice, apply as well to the leader of the Opposition ?
Mr. Mackenzie King: Hear, hear.
Mr. McMaster: I would have not the slightest objection to its applying to the leader of the Opposition.
Mr. Meighen: And to the leaders of both Oppositions?
Mr. Mackenzie King: Certainly.

Mr. McMaster: I know my own leader and can speak for him; I am sure he would not have the slightest objection to having it apply to him. As regards the leader of the Opposition sitting angularly opposite, I cannot speak for him.
Mr. Doherty: But does the principle apply?
Mr. McMaster: There is, of course, the consideration, as the member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) remarks, that there is no salary attached to the position of the leader of the other Opposition.
Mr. Meighen: That is not the point.
Mr. McMaster: That is not the great point,
I admit. If that is the only thing standing in the way of the Government's acceptance of my bill, I would be willing to go one step further and have it apply to the leader of the Opposition as well.
Mr. Meighen: It would be of no use to have the one without the other.
Mr. Mackenzie King: Perhaps I should say right at the moment that I should feel it distinctly in the public interest to have the provision apply to the leader of the Opposition.

625341,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.11.28,1922-04-24,b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5,ca.m.7719,Mr. MACKENZIE KING:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,MINISTERS AND DIRECTORSHIPS,,,Hear, hear.

,Liberal,,William Lyon Mackenzie King,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5&Language=E&Section=ALL
625342,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.11.29,1922-04-24,a8b2b613-dd5c-4a22-8f22-c0e4f180c7b6,ca.m.4552,Mr. GUTHRIE:,,MINISTERS AND DIRECTORSHIPS,,,My hon. friend now says, ""hear, hear."" I assume from that "" hear, hear "" that he has not changed his views during the intervening twelve months, and that he still applauds the same principle to-night. So I suppose we are going to find him in hearty accord and sympathy with the motion which my hon. friend from Brome has moved on this occasion.

But my hon. friend, the Prime Minister, has acted very strangely in the interval. In the meantime we had a general election, and my hon. friend was called upon to form a new government. In the few months that intervened he cannot have forgotten that debate which took place in March last year. That debate and his vote on that bill must have been present to his mind when His Excellency called upon him to form an administration. If these were his principles and his convictions then-and as he

column2: COMMONS

column1: Ministers and Directorships

hear hears "" them to-night when I refer to them, I assume they are still-then why did he so utterly disregard them when he undertook to form his administration? I turn to the division list on that bill, and I find no less than six ministers of the Crown sitting to-day on the Treasury benches, all of whom voted for that measure, that sweeping proposal introduced by my hon. friend from Brome in March, 1921; I find there my hon. friend, the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment (Mr. Beland), voting for that measure; I find my hon. friend, the Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau), among the names of those who voted for the bill; I find the name of my hon. friend, the Secretary of State (Mr. Copp), among those who voted for the measure; I find the name of my hon. friend, the Prime Minister, among the supporters of the measure; also my hon. friend, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe), and my hon. friend, the Solicitor General (Mr. McKenzie). All of them, solidly, upon that occasion, with great acclaim and enthusiasm declared to the House and the country their support of that radical and sweeping enactment which proposed that no man who was a director of any incorporated company could sit in the Cabinet. A few months afterwards a new government was formed, and I believe I am within the mark when I say that several members of that government are at this moment directors of incorporated companies. And not only that-that relates to the bill of last year-but they would likewise come within the narrower language of the motion this year, namely,

'that all ministers of the Crown, on their appointment as such, should resign afll directorships held by them in banks, trust companies, insurance companies, transportation companies or large public utility corporations;

It is strange, Mr. Speaker, that in one short year after a solemn pronouncement of that character-because a vote in this House, I take it, is about the most solemn pronouncement a man can make-my hon. friend, the leader of the Government should, at the very first opportunity, seek to violate and repudiate the principle which he then solemnly affirmed.
Now, for myself, I am not inclined to agree with my hon. friend from Brome in the proposal which he has so eloquently placed before the House this afternoon.

I believe he is making a mistake in his motion, that he is assuming too much in connection with our public life, and he has not in my opinion made out any case at all for action such as that contemplated

in his motion. I cast my view back over the last fifty or sixty years of our political history since the day when Canada became a Confederation, and I fail to recall a single instance where injury has resulted to the public service, to the government of the country, by reason of the fact that a minister of the Crown was likewise a director of an incorporated company. There may be an instance of the kind, but I have failed to recall it, and certain it is that my hon. friend from Brome did not cite such an instance, unless in the case of the Merchants Bank, which I will refer to in a moment. Coming from 1867 down to the present day, Mr. Speaker, I cannot recall a single instance where public injury has resulted from the fact that a minister of the Crown was also a director of an incorporated company. If after fifty or sixty years' experience we find there has been no lapse, no wrong, no public injury, then am I not within the mark when I say that my hon. friend from Brome is seeking to provide a remedy where there is no ailment?

What is the disease in the body politic which my hon. friend from Brome is seeking to cure? He has not explained to the House what the particular ailment or disease or wrong is; he has cited no instance at all. Therefore I submit he is dealing too much in the realm of possibilities rather than of probabilities. I do not believe wrong or injury has ensued, and I do not believe that wrong or injury will ensue to the public service or to the people of this country by reason of our continuing under the present law, which it seems to me affords every reasonable safeguard. The present law on the subject is in the House of Commons Act, which was quoted this afternoon by my hon. friend from Brome. That law has been in existence practically since Confederation. It applies not only to ministers, but to every hon. member of the House, and that law has up to the present, I submit, been sufficient. My hon. friend has failed to show that there is any rule on the subject, either in this Dominion or in Great Britain. There is some practice to be found in the Imperial Parliamentary reports, I admit, but the practice appears to be as much one way as it is the other. Purely from curiosity I have looked a little into the history of our Canadian Parliament in this respect, and I find that in every administration whether Conservative or Liberal, prominent members of the ministry have been closely identified with
Ministers and Directorships

great business undertakings in Canada. But I have found no lapse on that account. I take for example the government of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier; when I first came into this House over twenty years ago, Sir Wilfrid Laurier himself, then Prime Minister, was director of one of the great life insurance companies of this country, the Mutual Life of Canada. No one would suggest that this circumstance proved detrimental to the public service or to the people of Canada; quite the reverse, I can assure you. That particular company came to this Parliament for legislation during that period, but nobody ever suggested that the fact that Sir Wilfrid Laurier was a director of it had anything to do with the matter. I take the case of the late Mr. Sutherland, whom I knew very well. I turn to the Parliamentary Companion in regard to Mr. Sutherland, because I know that while members do not write the notices in that book, they have the opportunity of revising them, and, as a rule, statements found there are fairly accurate. I find that the late Mr. Sutherland, who was Minister of Public Works in the cabinet of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier was ""a director of several trading and commercial companies."" I turn to the name of the late Mr. Prefon-taine, Minister of Marine and Fisheries in that cabinet, and I find identically the same language: that he likewise was ""a director of several trading and commercial companies."" I turn to the name of Sir Richard Cartwright, and I find the following language in regard to him: ""He is president, director or trustee of several commercial and financial corporations."" We all remember Mr. Charles Hyman, at one time Minister of Public Works in that same administration, a man connected with a number of commercial companies and likewise a director of the Bank of Toronto. And so with the preceding Conservative administration:
column2: I take the name of Sir John Carling, connected with half a dozen joint stock companies and with one bank. I take the name of the late Sir Frank Smith, vicepresident of the Dominion Bank and president of transportation companies in Canada. You will find that the same thing applies practically to every government that has held office since confederation. But the point that I want to urge upon, the House is that so far as we know, so far as experience goes, so far as history goes, no harm has resulted from the practice, no wrong has been done by it. There has been no weakness in the system; no public injury has resulted from the system.

column1: Now, I believe in many cases it would be a very great hardship to ask a man, as the price of his admission into the government of this country-a man who is wanted in that capacity-that he forego his right to sit on a board of directors in any of the companies enumerated in this motion, and in which his whole fortune may be wrapped up. It may be his whole investment; his life's work may be represented in the capital stock of that company of which he is a director. His presence may be urgently required in the government of Canada, and it would be a hardship-to my mind it would be an absurdity-to ask him to come in and assist in the government of the country and at the same time to say to him: If you do, you must jeopardize your private fortune and resign your directorship. That, simply, is the proposal of the present resolution.

I said at the outset that I believed my hon. friend from Brome had distinctly failed to make out a case for changing the law. If he were able to make out such a case, then I might revise my opinion, but up to the present, I am satisfied, he has failed to make out a case. He seeks to produce a remedy for a disease which is non-existent in the history of the government of Canada and has been from confederation up to the present time. However, I am satisfied that what the House and the country most desire to know at the moment is what view the Prime Minister of Canada takes on this question. I know there is great expectation in the galleries; I know there is great expectation in the country-one has only to read the daily press and to see the names there mentioned and the views there expressed to realize that-and there is a general subdued excitement and curiosity to know just what the Prime Minister intends to do in regard to this matter. I can tell the hon. member for Brome that if this resolution were to pass it might have one very unfortunate application in regard to this Government and this country. True, it would not be in the nature of an enactment upon our statute book, but it would be a resolution of the House of Commons, tantamount to a plain direction of this body which any government is bound to obey. If the resolution passed this House, the Government would be expected to obey it, and we might be placed in the position of being called upon to sacrifice an hon. member of the Government whom we on this side of the House look upon, and whom a great many of the people in this country look upon, as about the only real guarantee
Ministers and Directorships

of stability which the Government contains. I refer of course to my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin). If the passage of this motion as it stands to-day were to put the Minister of Justice to an election in the matter; if it were to call upon him to decide whether he should resign his position in the Government or his position as director of the various banks or companies of which he now is director, and if he should decide to resign his position in the Government, I will be candid enough to say that I believe it would be nothing short of a calamity in the country at the present critical juncture of our national affairs. It would be a most unfortunate thing for the country, to say the least, but for the Government itself it would be a positive catastrophe. It is no wonder that there is considerable expectation in the House and in the country as to just what the leader of the Government intends to do in regard to this motion, and perhaps the easiest way to find that out is for me to conclude my remarks and allow him to inform us.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Hugh Guthrie,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=a8b2b613-dd5c-4a22-8f22-c0e4f180c7b6&Language=E&Section=ALL
625343,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.11.30,1922-04-24,b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5,ca.m.7719,Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) :,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,MINISTERS AND DIRECTORSHIPS,,,Mr. Speaker, I must thank

my hon. friend (Mr. Guthrie) who has just taken his seat for the compliment he has paid me in saying that the views which I have to express with regard to this motion are of more than exceptional interest to himself and to other members of the House, and possibly also to the country generally. I shall endeavour to leave no doubt in the mind of my hon. friend or of any person in this country as to where I stand with regard to the resolution now before the House.

Let me say first of all that I conceive the purpose of the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) in introducing his motion, to be that of helping to bring about in the mind of the public generally, a greater sense of security in the administration of public affairs, irrespective of the government that may be carrying on the business of the country. So far as his motion is calculated to have that effect-to give to the public a sense of greater security in the administration of the day-I am certainly in hearty accord with my hon friend. But so far as his motion is calculated, to create in the minds of the people a distrust in or suspicion of the Government, when there is no just cause or good reason for such distrust or suspicion, I am entirely opposed to the motion.

My hon. friend has said, and I think very wisely, that in a matter of great importance such as this we may well be guided by British practice and British procedure. He has stated that we need not slavisly follow all that is done by the Mother of Parliaments on the other side of the water. Nevertheless, he has wisely affirmed that the British Parliament affords to parliamentary assemblies possibly the safest guide of any institution in the world as to what is best in maintaining the highest and noblest traditions. Having this in mind, with such assistance as I have been able to get from recognized constitutional authorities, from books, and from students of this question, I have gone to some pains to endeavour to see what attitude the British Parliament has taken on this all important question. I shall seek to compress into a very few paragraphs the essence of the situation as it has been of recent years.

May I say first of all, that when this question has come up for discussion in the British Parliament it has generally been viewed from a much broader point of view than the restricted one of the present motion, which is limited to the question of directors relinquishing their directorships upon entering the Government. The question has generally heen discussed from the broad point of view of the right of members to vote where they are believed to have a personal interest in the subject matter which is before the House. That question has been debated over and over again in the British Parliament. It has been the subject of special parliamentary inquiries. My hon. friend this afternoon quoted some illustrious names in support of a contention which he was making. I hold in my hand a report of the Select Committee of the British Parliament on this personal interest matter, together with the proceedings of the committee, etc. The report was made in the year 1890, and I find in the membership of the committee such illustrious names as Sir Michael Hicks-Beach, Mr. Campbell-Bannerman, Mr. Courtney, Mr. Haldane, Mr. Lloyd George, and several others. This committee, having examined carefully the rules of the House to discover whether it was advisable to extend them in any way for the purpose of affording greater security in the public mind as to votes cast in the House of Commons, came to the conclusion that the rules as they stood at the time were to all intents and purposes sufficient.
Ministers and Directorships

May I say that judging from the records of the British House of Commons, it would appear that while at all times it has been admitted that members of the House have a right to question the right of any other member to vote on a particular matter in which he is supposed to have a personal interest, yet whenever that vote has been taken, with the exception of possibly one or two cases out of a very large number, the House of Commons of Great Britain has invariably decided that the matter should be regarded as one of honour and conscience on the part of the member who is casting his vote, and has refused to deny him the right of voting.

I contend Sir, that that is the right point of view from which to view this question, but coming to the more restricted view, that namely of the duty of members of a government to relinquish their directorships, I find that there have been, broadly speaking, four different attitudes. The first I might describe as an attitude of indifference towards this subject; no question whatever being raised on the subject. I take it that this attitude is not entirely a matter of chance or of accident. I think there are good and sufficient reasons why the British House of Commons has for the most part assumed it. A good and sufficient reason, to my mind, is that every minister of the Crown has in the first instance been elected to Parliament by the people of his constituency. His associations, financial and commercial, are known to his electors, and if they are of a character to arouse suspicion or distrust, then they may become a matter of discussion on the public platform, and, indeed, are certain to be if they are likely to be in any serious way a matter of grave concern.
I would point out further, that

9 p.m. a member of Parliament once he becomes a minister of the Crown, is obliged to resign his seat and to return to his constituency for re-election. He has to go through the process of twice appealing to the electors. The electors know when they are choosing him in the first place whether he is a director of financial concerns or not; when he goes back for re-election as a cabinet minister they also know whether he is a director or not. If his associations are likely to prove detrimental to the discharge of his public duties, that is the time when protest should be made. That is the time when public opinion, which is the last resort in all these matters, should make itself felt.

Let me mention next an attitude at the opposite extreme. I have spoken of the attitude of indifference. There is also the attitude of statutory prohibition, very much the attitude of my hon. friend who has moved this resolution, because I take it that a resolution of the House of Commons to all intents and purposes is expected to have the effect of legislation. My hon. friend referred this afternoon to an hon. member of the British Parliament, Mr. Swift MacNeil, who introduced into the House of Commons in England a measure very much along the line of his own resolution. Not only did Mr. Swift MacNeil introduce such a measure on one occasion, but he introduced it, I think, at least a dozen times, and on every occasion the House of Commons of Great Britain refused to pass that resolution. That is the attitude which the English Parliament has taken towards the extreme of statutory prohibition with respect to ministers of the Crown holding directorates.

The third attitude is the one which has been taken by Mr. Balfour, Lord Salisbury, and other Conservative leaders when this matter came up for discussion. They have contended that these questions should be regarded as matters of conscience and honour, that it should be left to every public man to be guided in his actions as a cabinet minister and as a member of Parliament by the dictates of his conscience and as his own sense of honour would seem to render proper. In the long run we will gain more in virility in our public life by leaving some matters to conscience and honour rather than by seeking to enforce prohibitions that may be too severe and too drastic, and in the end only have the effect of bestowing harsh moral judgments upon some of our fellowmen.

The fourth attitude is the one which I might describe as the Gladstone-Camp-bell-Bannerman-Asquith attitude, which has been to adopt, not as a written rule, not as a matter of legislation, but as a matter of unwritten policy, subject always to exceptions where exceptions seem to be justifiable, the attitude that ministers of the Crown should not retain directorships. That has been the attitude which has been taken by most of the English Liberal statesmen. That attitude is one on which I shall say a few more words a little later on. It is not, as I have mentioned, the enforcement by resolution of the House of Commons, but rather leaving it to the Prime Minister to exercise his judgment in the formation of his Cabinet as to what
Ministers and Directorships
may be most in the public interest and what is best for the nation under the existing circumstances.

So much, then, for the attitude which the British House of Commons has taken. I think if we are to follow British practice in any particular, we would be justified also in following British procedure in the manner of putting that practice into play. If we are to make prevail in this country an opinion such as is suggested in the motion of my hon. friend, I think it is much better that it should be left to a prime minister, in consultation with his colleagues, to take the course which the public interest seems to dictate as wisest and best, all circumstances being considered, rather than to tie the hands of a prime minister and to fetter his government by restrictions which do not take account of circumstances which in the public interest should be taken account of.

My hon. friend this afternoon gave several reasons in support of his motion, and with them I should like to deal. First of all, let me say, I can conceive of cases where it would be very much against the interests of the public for certain individuals to hold cabinet positions and at the same time retain directorships in certain companies. My hon. friend has cited an example this afternoon that I think might well be put forward as a case in point. There are times when certain measures are under consideration, as was cited to-day, where ministers might well feel it the part of propriety, to resign their directorships or else resign from the ministry. But I think these cases have to be treated on their merits, and I submit that nothing has arisen in connection with the present administration which gives any ground to any one for believing that such circumstance exists in this country at this time.

My hon. friend has spoken about a possible conflict of fiduciary interests. He has pointed out that ministers of the Crown have to give most of their time to the business of government, and, I think, last year he said that he believed, where there was a conflict between an hon. member's time as devoted to public affairs and given to private affairs, private, not public, affairs were likely to suffer. That may be a good reason why companies might find it in their interests, perhaps, to prohibit their directors from taking positions in governments, but I do not think it is an equally strong reason why the country should be denied the service of men who have risen high

in financial and commercial confidence, if the companies with which they are associated are prepared to allow these gentlemen to give their services to the country in dealing with great national, financial and commercial affairs.

Similarly, my hon. friend spoke about the danger of interlocking directorates. There may be an evil in interlocking directorates, but I contend that the way to meet and cure that evil is not to pass an enactment which will prevent a director of any public company coming into a government without resigning his directorship. Let us deal with the evil of interlocking directorates, as such.

My hon. friend said that he was only following existing legislation. I should like for a moment to invite the attention of the House to the existing legislation, because I can well believe that there are members in this House to-day who may think that there is not adequate legislation to protect the public interests where an hon. member who has to do with affairs of government is connected also with a business which may have direct or indirect dealings with the Government in a manner which will be furthering special interests rather than public interests. I contend that if we read carefully the legislation that at present exists in the Act respecting the Senate and the House of Commons referring more particularly to the independence of members of Parliament we will find that the interests of the public, as respects members of Parliament who are directors and members of a government, is pretty well taken care of in that legislation as my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) has already said. Let me read section 14 of the act, and ask hon. gentlemen to recollect that, inasmuch as it applies to every member of Parliament, it applies equally to every minister of the Crown, since every minister of the Crown is already a member of Parliament. The section reads:

No person, directly or indirectly, alone or with any other, by himself or by the interposition of any trustee or third party, holding or enjoying, undertaking or executing any contract or agreement, expressed or implied, with or for the Government of Canada on behalf of the Crown, or with or for any of the officers of the Government of Canada, for which any public money of Canada is to be paid, shall be eligible as a member of the House of Commons, or shall sit or vote in the said House.
Can legislation be more emphatic than that? If we live up to that legislation, what
Ministers and Directorships

likelihood is there of any director of a company, through his position in the cabinet, doing anything unfair or unjust which could be prevented by legislation such as my hon. friend has suggested. Then take the next section, No. 15-

If any member of the House of Commons accepts any office or commission, or is concerned or interested in any contract, agreement, service or work which, by this Act, renders a person incapable of being elected to, or of sitting or voting in the House of Commons, or knowingly sells any goods, wares or merchandise to, or performs any service for the Government of Canada, or for any of the officers of the Government of Canada, for which any public money of Canada is paid or to be paid, whether such contract, agreement or sale is expressed or implied, and whether the transaction is single or continuous, the seat of such member shall thereby be vacated, and his election shall be thenceforth null and void.
But let me direct attention specially to section 21, which, I think, is even more important-

No member of the Senate or of the House of Commons shall receive or agree to receive any compensation, directly or indirectly, fdr services rendered, or to be rendered, to any person, either by himself or another, in relation to any bill, proceeding, contract, claims, controversy, charge, accusation, arrest, or other matter before the Senate or the House of Commons, or before a Committee of either House, or in order to influence or to attempt to influence any member of either House.
Subsection 2 reads:-

Every member of the Senate offending against this section shall be liable to a fine of not less than one thousand dollars and not more than four thousand dollars, and every member of the House of Commons offending against this section shall be liable to a fine of not less than five hundred dollars and not more than two thousand dollars, and shall for five years after conviction of such offence be disqualified from being a member of the House of Commons, and from holding any office in the public service of Canada.
Subsection 3 reads:

Any person who gives, offers or promises to any such member any compensation for such services as aforesaid, rendered or to be rendered, is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to one year's imprisonment and to a fine of not less than five hundred dollars and not more than two thousand dollars.

May I not ask members of this House, is it possible to conceive of any hon. gentleman, being a director and using his position in a government in a manner to further the interests of a company with which he is concerned, who would not become liable to lose his seat in the House of Commons under this legislation? And would not the companies with which he was concerned, if they sought to influence him through payment of director's fees or in any other manner, be violating the law of this country as it stands at the present time?

May I say a further word in regard to one or two other references of my hon. friend? He spoke of the judges of the country and said that the law requires that the judges must give their whole time to the work in which they are engaged and, in the discharge of their judicial duties; must not accept directorships. May I remind my hon. friend that judges are appointed for life; they are given a life tenure of office. They hold their positions at good salaries, with the expectation that their time will be given for the remainder of their days to the discharge of judicial duties. No such undertaking can be given with respect to members of a government.

I only need to look opposite to see half a dozen gentlemen who entered the cabinet of my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) shortly before the last general election. They were in office for about three months, and, that is all they will ever see of office in the course of their lives. How unfair it would have been to these gentlemen to say ""You shall not enter the Government without giving up your directorships in any companies you belong to,"" and then for them to find, at the end of the few weeks they had served their country in the capacity of cabinet ministers, that they had not only ceased to be cabinet ministers, but had severed any connection they had ever had with any company. The comparison of my hon. friend in regard to judges is not a true parallel by a very long degree.

My hon. friend spoke of the members of the Railway Commission. There again, we have a definite position that is fixed in tenure for a period of years. But if my hon. friend will look at the references to the Railway Commissioners, he will find that they are not precluded from being directors of all public companies. They are precluded from being directors of railway companies, or any companies with which railways are likely to have business dealings-a very proper and right thing in every way. But this is not any such sweeping, wholesale, self-denying ordinance as my hon. friend seeks to impose upon individuals who may enter a government as cabinet ministers.
The hon. member for Brome (Mr. Mc-Master) spoke of the Secretary of the Treasury in the United States and said that he noticed, following the best practice in the United States, that Mr. Secre-
Ministers and Directorships

tary Mellon had resigned directorships that he held in companies. I do not know whether my hon. friend is aware of the fact or not; but I am informed that in the United States there is a special law applicable to the Secretary of the Treasury alone, not to any other minister, and that under that law the Secretary of the Treasury has resigned such positions as he has held on boards of directors. I am inclined to think the example of our country in that respect is even better than that of the United States. The Minister of Finance is necessarily brought into very close relation with many industrial concerns. My hon. friend said that the exMinister of Finance, Sir Thomas White, resigned his directorships when he became Minister of Finance. That was taking a view of his obligations as Minister of Finance voluntarily, not in view of any statute, and that is a much finer attitude for any hon. gentleman to take than to be obliged to do something by compulsion. The House well knows that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) in the present Administration holds no directorships in any companies having anything to do with the business of this country. But I venture to say that there is not in this country a man who would have any less confidence in the minister if he held directorships in twenty companies. Public confidence is a matter of belief in the integrity and honesty of a man and not of the position that he may hold. You may have a man without any position who is thoroughly dishonourable; you may have another man holding a dozen positions who, for the very reason that he has a greater responsibility, feels that his integrity must be so much the more circumspectly guarded.

There is this aspect also which is worthy of consideration. The motion of my hon. friend does not go so far as to say that shareholders, if they enter a government as cabinet ministers, must give up their shares in companies. I will leave it to the judgment of the House, from the point of view of public interest as to which is the better-to have a gentleman in a cabinet who is a shareholder in a company, but who is also a director and known to the world as a director, or to have a gentleman in a cabinet having large shareholdings in one of these public companies of which the public knows nothing because of his not being a director? I contend that the mere fact that a gentleman is known to be a director of a particular

corporation places upon him a special obligation to be particularly careful when any matter affecting the business of the corporation with which he is associated comes up for consideration in the Cabinet.

'[DOT] Men of a high sense of honour will take good care, to see that when matters concerning companies with which they are concerned come up for consideration in Cabinet or Parliament, when there is the slightest possibility of their integrity or honesty being challenged, to vacate or withdraw while the discussion is going on and the matter is being settled.

The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) quoted from Hansard of last year as to my position in the discussion which took place at that time. With respect to what I said in the debate of last year, I have not a single word to withdraw. I wish to reiterate at the present moment every word that I said on that occasion. At that time I was leader of the Opposition.

625345,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.11.32,1922-04-24,b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5,ca.m.7719,Mr. MACKENZIE KING:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,MINISTERS AND DIRECTORSHIPS,,,Those words seem to belong to the position of leader of the Opposition, because they are exactly the ones I used last year at the particular time:
Mr. Meighen: Does the hon. member not think that it his bill is to be accepted, it should, under our present practise, apiply as well to the leader of the Opposition?
Mr. Mackenzie King: Hear, hear.
Just what my right hon. friend has said, sitting in exactly the same spot. Further:
Mr. Meighen: And members leaders ot both oppositions.
Mr. Mackenzie King: Certainly.
I made one other reference in the debate, and it was this:
Perhaps I should say right at the moment that I should feel it distinctly in the public interest to have the provision apply to the leader of the Opposition.

I stated that, when I was leader of the Opposition. I thought it would be in the public interest that a leader of a political party should not have any associations with corporations by way of directorships and I take that position now. I think my right hon. friend opposite to me takes the same position; I think both he and I hold similar views on these matters. I think each of us has refrained from accepting directorships in any companies. Why? Not because we thought it was wrong that we should accept or that other men should accept directorships, or because we
Ministers and Directorships

thought men should not accept positions as ministers of the Crown while holding directorships, but because as leaders of parties, officially so recognized by the law of the country, we regarded our position as perhaps the more secure in the minds of our following as well as of the country, in taking that particular attitude. I wish to repeat that I think it is in the public interest that leaders of great political parties should in every way possible seek to give their entire time and thought to their public duties, and to put their position as far as possible beyond any possibility of question by their own following or by the public generally.
The hon. member for South Wellington went one step further. He said:
column2: Why

column1: did I forget all about the position that I took in the debate when I came to form the new administration? I did not forget the position that I had taken at that time. I remembered it very distinctly and I remembered also the vote which was registered in this House at that time and which was to the effect that that bill should not carry. The House of Commons, when this subject was up for debate before, decided against the principle that it was not advisable that hon. members holding positions as directors should be admitted as ministers of the Crown. I repeat, I can conceive of cases where it would not be in the public interest for certain gentlemen holding directorships to be simultaneously ministers of the Crown. I believe a situation of that character will make itself apparent, and become quickly apparent, to any one accustomed to dealing with public affairs. But I can also see where the passing of a resolution such as is proposed by my hon. friend to-night, might deprive the country of the services of some of the ablest business men in Canada and this at a time when special knowledge of financial and commercial conditions is most needed in the management of public affairs. I am free to admit that I was confronted with that very problem when called upon to form the present administration. The member for Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) has spoken of the hon. the Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin). May I tell the House exactly what took place between the Minister of Justice and myself when I asked that hon. gentleman if he would become a member of the cabinet? When I approached him with the invitation to join the cabinet he said, in reply, that he had been a long time in public life, and had left it with the intention of retiring for

good; that he had had no thought of going back into Parliament and resuming the burdens which cabinet responsibility places upon one who has rendered many years of public service; that, having regard to the vicissitudes of public life, its uncertainties and its obligations, he would hesitate to enter the Government if it meant severing his financial and commercial associations.

I told him I thought the country appreciated the distinguished service which he had rendered not only to his own province, in the position of Prime Minister, for fifteen years, but to the whole Dominion of Canada as well; that he was everywhere recognized as outstanding in the country's affairs. I said that the people of Canada wanted and needed his services, and that I would not think of pressing an individual opinion in matters of this kind as against the judgment of himself or any of my colleagues in the present administration. Had I, regardless of their distinction and public service, sought to impose upon hon gentlemen coming into the cabinet restrictions of various kinds, I might have succeeded in effecting a mediocre administration; I certainly would not have had the privilege of being surrounded to-day by the gentlemen of distinction and eminence whc sit in the cabinet. There are times and places for everything. I have spoken of the Gladstone, the Campbell-Bannerman, and, if you will, the Asquith tradition. May I remind my hon. friend that it was 1868 when Mr. Gladstone first became Prime Minister of England. He was then 59 years of age, and had had a long parliamentary experience. It was not until 1892, a quarter of a century afterwards, when he was past 80 years of age, that Mr. Gladstone sought to impose any self-denying ordinances upon his colleagues. If my hon. friend will give me time, and the occasion demands it, I shall be glad to follow the Gladstonian tradition. I think it would come with much better grace from an older to younger men, than from a young man to men who have long served the country with distinction, and with great honour and credit to themselves and to their nation, to lay down rules in the nature of self-denying ordinances which after all might serve only to indicate a lack of confidence in their fidelity and integrity. As between myself and my colleagues, and between the Government and the country, the relationship I wish to have maintained is that of ""Trust me all in all, or not at all."" That is the attitude I hold towards
Ministers and Directorships

every member of the Government, and it is the attitude I believe which every member of the Government holds towards myself. While we began with confidence in each other's integrity and ability, I may say that at this moment that confidence has ripened into implicit trust. Inasmuch as the support of my hon. friend's motion would seem to make it necessary for me to reflect upon the honour and the integrity of any hon. gentlemen associated with me in the cabinet, I must decline absolutely to vote for it.
