ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):,Leader of the Official Opposition,MINISTERS AND DIRECTORSHIPS,,,If the experience of the last two months had not rendered me utterly impervious to all sentiments of amazement, it would require at least the space of a few half hours to recover sufficiently from the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in order to address this House. I thought that the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) was rendering a service when, in speaking on the motion, he invited, even prodded, the leader of the Government to make a statement on behalf of the administration, and to seek to harmonize opposition to this resolution with his vote of a year ago. Well, my hon. friend in so doing may have contributed a service to the country, but he contributed none to the Government and in all respect I suggest that the reputation of the Prime Minister would have been infinitely better if he had declined to yield to the invitation of the member for Wellington and had maintained a discreet if not a dignified silence.

What is the resolution that we are asked now to vote upon? The hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) moves that legislation should be enacted providing that no member of a government of Canada shaTl be a director of any of four classes of companies: first, banks, second, trust companies, third, insurance companies, and fourth, transportation companies to which is added in general words a fifth, large public utility corporations; and that, should a member of a government be a director of any company other than those recited, that company should be debarred from all business with the country. Now, the resolution, admits of discussion from two phases: first, as to its intrinsic merits;-should it be supported or be defeated? Secondly, the resolution is important to the House as bearing upon the public honour of the country, as impersonated in the government in
office, I shall commence by discussing the question from the first standpoint.

A year ago the same hon. member, in a speech ranking, perhaps, not equal in fullness of treatment, but ranking equal in fairness and dignity, with that delivered today, introduced and urged to second reading, not a resolution merely, but a bill, a statute, providing that no member of the government should under any consideration be a director of any company whatever. That resolution was pressed in this House, supported by several hon. members, and resisted by several, including myself; and, on its coming to a decision, a majority vote against it was recorded. I took the stand then that this was a question that could not be adequately or fairly decided by statutory enactment; that is to say, that it would not be possible for this House to enact legislation which would deal fairly with the situation, which would be practical on the one hand and beneficial on the other. I argued that for the House to enact that a member of a government should not be a director of any company was in effect to debar from the public service many of the business community who could render distinct, indeed conspicuous, service to the state; and, further, that such an enactment would secure no commensurate result. I contended that, to pass the bill which the hon. member moved would, while debarring directors of companies, at the same time admit to the public service as members of the government those who could be influenced by exactly the same considerations, but who might not be directors of companies. On several grounds, by myself and others, it was urged that you could not deal with this evil-if, indeed, it was an evil at all-by statutory enactment, but that, in the words of the then hon. member for Red Deer, Mr. Clark, who delivered a speech that I commend to the consideration of hon. members, it was fundamentally, historically and necessarily a matter for the conscience and honour of the minister himself. That is the stand I took then; that is the stand I take to-day.

I pointed out at that time that if you legislated to debar an hon. member from being a director of a company and also a minister of the crown, you would put it out of the power of a man who had made some money, incorporated a company, and required to exercise some little supervision over the competence that he had gathered for the taking care of his family after his death by being director of his company-
Ministers and Directorships

you would, I said, put it absolutely out of the* power of that man to be admitted to a share in government, while at the same time the man who did exactly the same thing, who had his company not incorporated but a mere personal concern, could be a member of the government and could as well devote such time as he thought fit to the affairs of his company.

That result in the first place would be unfair. I remember it being urged very strongly by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb) - who, let me say, is the sole conspicuous example of anything approaching consistency on this question among hon. members of the government-that to refuse a director admission to the Government would merely put a premium upon the practice of a director of a company in which he was largely interested appointing a mere dummy, his stenographer for instance, to be a director in his place, who in effect would be nothing but the mouthpiece of her principal and, consequently doing the will of the real director; his interest being concealed behind his dummy while he, the principal, took his place in the government. Many other objections were urged as well. It was instanced that you might have a man a director of a company who had a very minor interest in it, while some other man, not a director, might be interested to a very great extent. The first man is a director because of his acceptability, because of his business probity, because he is known and honoured of men; the other man is not a director, because although he is very rich he does not enjoy the confidence of the other shareholders, he does not enjoy the same reputation in the community. Under the law then suggested by the hon. member for Brome the second man, the unworthy man, could be a member of the government; but the man of honour, the man who stood out and made known to the world his position, was denied admission to the service of the state.

On other grounds the incongruity, the anomaly, the unfairness of the bill was clearly demonstrated to this House, but all to no effect. To no effect upon hon. members now sitting on the Treasury benches it was urged that in Great Britain from time immemorial it had never been the practice to deal with this matter by statutory enactment at all; that the British practice had been to leave the decision in each individual case to the honour, to the conscience, to the sense of public duty of

the minister himself, and that to this day there is no enactment in Great Britain along the lines of the bill of the hon. member for Brome introduced last session, or along the lines of his resolution to-night. All in vain it was urged-even urged by myself-that throughout the history of our provinces in not one of them had it ever been seen fit to enact legislation such as that proposed by the hon. member for Brome. There is just as much, yea, there is even more need for this legislation-if need exists at all-in our provincial legislatures than in this House, for our provincial legislatures have to do with those questions of property and civil rights that concern the welfare of companies, corporations, and individuals more directly than has this House. None of our legislatures, I say, has seen fit to follow this example. The idea sounds well, it perhaps makes some appeal to certain people. But it has been considered unsound historically in Great Britain, it has been considered unsound historically in this Dominion, and none of our provinces, whether under Liberal rule, whether under Conservative rule,-yes, though under Progressive rule, has ever seen fit to propose such legislation. These were the arguments urged against the measure. Those arguments appealed to me; many of them I advanced myself. All these arguments I stand by to-night as leader of the Opposition just as I stood by them as leader of the Government.

Now, the resolution before the House is much milder, it is true, than the bill of a year ago. The hon. member for Brome, influenced, he says, by the arguments then advanced, has reduced the scope of his proposal. He says: ""I won't object any longer to a member of the Government being a director of an industrial corporation; I won't object any longer to a member of the Government being a director even of a loan company; I won't object any more to a member of the Government being a director of a great manufacturing enterprise, the arguments of last year have put those ideas out of my head and behind me; but I say that after this, if I have my way, no member of the Government shall be a director of a bank, nor of a trust company, nor of a transportation company, nor of an insurance company, nor of a public utility corporation.""
Now, that I may be perfectly clear, let me say before commencing my argument on this resolution, that I am equally op-
Ministers and Directorships

posed to it as I was to his bill last year. The hon. member's resolution indeed illustrates, as nothing could illustrate better, the inherent unsoundness and fatuousness of the bill of last year, and as well of the method he is adopting now to gain the end he seeks. For what is going to be the result if legislation is introduced confirmatory of this resolution? A director of the British Empire Steel Corporation could still be a member of the government-that would be perfectly all right; a director of the Massey-Harris Company could be a member of the government-that would be all right; a director of the Dominion Textile Company

instead of representing us at an economic conference-could be a member of the government; indeed, we might have, as the hon. member frankly admitted, sixteen presidents of textile companies composing the government if his resolution passed and a bill confirmatory of it was enacted. But if a man is a director of the Street Railway Company of the town of Guelph, he could not be a member of the government; if he is a director of an old corporation, that is all but dead save in name, that once proposed to build a street railway in Portage La Prairie, his interest would be such that the door must be shut against his admission to high place in public life; a director of any little transportation concern, though it be half dead and half alive, anywhere in this Dominion, could not for the life of him get into the government. But a man may be president of British Empire Steel; he may be president of the Dominion Coal Company; he may be president of Dominion Textiles; he may be president of Massey-Harris; he may be president or director of the Cockshutt Company, and he still will be all right and quite fit for admission to the Administration. Now, I know the difficulty the hon. member confronted. He concluded-the argument was such he could not help it

that you could not shut the door to public life and admission to the ministry to those engaged in industrial enterprises. He knew that a man would thereby be debarred from exercising openly, which is always far better than secretly, such supervision of the money as he has managed to make in his life, that he owes to his family, owes to his descendants; and that if you debar public men of that right you cannot expect men of consequence to enter public life. It is just because of this difficulty which the hon. member eon-tMr Metehen.l

fronted, and which is reflected in this reduced and wholly illogical resolution that he introduces to-day-it is just for that reason that it has been found impossible in all countries to take care of this evil, if it is evil at all, by statutory enactment. Therefore the argument on this point by the Prime Minister to-night had some appeal to me. I almost congratulated myself that if what I said a year ago passed then like cold water from his breast, if all my arguments had fallen at that time upon barren soil, at least I could see that there had been a fertilizing process in the interval and that what I had sowed in good season was maturing into harvest now.

Let us for a moment, in all seriousness, refer to that phase of the question that has to do with the public honour of our country as embodied and illustrated in the ministry of the day. A year ago a sweeping, all-embracing bill is put before this Parliament for final decision. Arguments are adduced pro and con, just as have been adduced to-night. The government of the day opposes the measure. The government of the day gains a little, but very little, support in its negation from the Opposition of that time, also from the Progressive party of that time. There may have been others, but I recall the leader of the Progressive party, the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) and the hon. member for Red Deer supporting the government in its opposition. But against' the course the government took, the leader of the present Government stood and voted, and every indication of opinion that he made was to the effect that he not only favoured the bill but would go further than the bill went and would include within its sweep the leader of the Progressive party and the leader of the Opposition as well. That was the declaration of principle and of faith that the present leader of the Government made to this Dominion, and upon which among other things he appealed to the electorate for support. ""Oh,"" he often declared, ""I put the Government on its record,"" Very well; the Government stood on its record

did he stand on his? Is he standing on it tonight? I am afraid my resources of ridicule would be entirely insufficient if I came to examine the reasons that the leader of the Government advances. He says: ""Yes, it is true I supported this bill a year ago."" He did all right-he did more; he supported a bill that was sweeping, drastic and complete, going a great deal further than this
Ministers and Directorships

resolution goes. He declared that he wanted it to go even further. ""Oh, yes,"" he says, *""I voted for it, but I have kept in mind ever since the fact that the House voted it down."" ""I remember well how I voted, I have never forgotten that,"" he assures the hon. member for Wellington, ""but I am not forgetting that the House voted it down. I declared my principles; I declared my belief; I submitted to this nation where I stood upon the question, but-save the mark-I cannot stand there any longer, because the House voted it down."" Well, this will come surely with a thud of despair to those hon. members of this House, if any are left, who expect the present administration under the present Prime Minister to adhere to anything they have declared for in the last five years. Did not the House vote them all down? There have been tariff resolutions proposed on the faith of which hon. gentlemen to my left have on many a platform proclaimed that the Liberal party were practically the same as they, and upon the faith of which hon. gentlemen opposite, with still more emphasis, have declared to the people that there was no need at all for the Progressive party because its principles were identical with their own. Tariff resolution after tariff resolution has been defeated by this House, proposed by hon. gentlemen opposite when they were in opposition, proposed by the present Prime Minister himself. Now, what are we to expect? When the Budget comes down and the vote of the hon. Prime Minister is held before his face, and the vote of his colleagues around him are shown all in black and white-when resolutions are called to his memory declaring for reductions on this thing and on that thing, all to cure unemployment and bring relief to a wearied and oppressed people

when all this is done, the Prime Minister will rise and say: ""Yes, I remember all these resolutions; I remember that I proposed them; I remember that I voted for them; I remember too, that I believed in them, but all is so different now, because those resolutions were voted down."" But more: ""Now,"" he says, ""I stand on British precedent."" May I ask what precedent he stood on a year ago? He has spent a lot of time on the subject; he has analysed the argument presented by the hon. member for Brome. Back centuries he has gone, and he divides into four categories all of those who have ever discussed this question in the British House. Some Who have discussed it, he says, are indifferent to it altogether-do not care anything about it. Others who have discussed it believe it should be left to conscience and to honour. Others, on the contrary, believe that there can be nothing done about it, even though they are not indifferent. And the fourth class, the Gladstone-in-his-prime class and the Campbell-Bannerman class-they believe that the decision should be left to the Prime Minister of the country; and of course my hon. friend, now that he is Prime Minister of the country, is right step in step with the Bannermans and the Gladstones, believing it should all be left to himself. I really admired the skill; rather I admired the plenitude of verbosity with which the hon. Prime Minister contrived to have this question lost in the fogs of the past, to have it buried in the recesses of history. How much better his memory was of what Gladstone said, of what Campbell-Bannerman said or of what Balfour said, than of What he said himself. How much better his memory was of the decisions of the British House and of debates in the House of Lords in the time of Pitt and Walpole than of the debate last March in the Commons of Canada and of his own vote on that occasion.

Oh,"" he said, ""when I came to form my Government I found out that my individual opinion should not prevail."" Why, he had told us before that he had abandoned his opinion in deference to the decision of this House. Which of his two statements is right. I am inclined to think the conclusion is that he has no opinion, and never had any real opinion; inded, I think those words apply to him as respects almost every subject of public policy in this country. ""I found,"" he says, ""that if I stood by that resolution I would have only a mediocre government; I could not form an administration of the conspicuous abilities of the hon. members who sit around me now.""

I might have had a government of Sinclairs and of Motherwells, if I may abandon the rule for a moment, but I could not have had for example the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau), I could not have had the hon. Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin), and I could not have had the Solicitor General (Mr. McKenzie). I could not have had such men as the hon. minister without portfolio from Quebec (Mr. Dan-durand), I could not have had the minister without portfolio from Renfrew (Mr. Low), nor could I have had my distinguished friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Kennedy). All these great men, six or seven
Ministers and Directorships

or eight, perhaps more, directors of companies and members of his government today he would have had to leave out of his cabinet, and because he had to decide between their superhuman capacities and his principles, without a moment's hesitation he abandoned his principles.

Now I stated a year ago that this is essentially a question to be left to the sense of self-respect and public respect of the member of the government himself. I stated a year ago that the matter had no personal reference to myself nor to the then leader of the Opposition, who is now Prime Minister, that neither of us had any directorships at all; but I stated as well that one could conceive of conditions where the intimacy of relationship between a membership of the governmnt and a directorship would be such that such directorship should not be held. I ask hon. members of the Government opposite simply to reflect whether there are not examples within their own household, rather remarkable examples that could be cured by the application of that sense of public respect and of public duty. I leave it to their own sense of honour and to their own conscience, just as I was prepared to leave it to the same in the case of the colleagues of whom I had the honour to be the head. But while I do so, is there anyone who as a Canadian can think quite the same of the Government of his country, yea, even of his country, when he finds today in that Government are members who are directors of companies and voted a year ago that it was a cardinal principle that no member of his government should be a director of a company. Six or seven or eight of those ministers I say are today directors of companies. The leader of the Government voted that it was in his judgment an evil to be immediately cured by legislation that a member of the Government should be the director of a company, and then immediately takes into his government six or seven or eight men and never asks one of them to surrender a directorship that he holds. Oh, he said, that was my opinion then and something like that was once the opinion of Gladstone, but poor old Gladstone was eighty years of age when he came to the conviction that a director of a company should not be a member of a government. That was, he suggests, the opinion of Gladstone in his senility. Well, the hon. member was not eighty years of age when a year ago he came to the same conclusion.
In process of time he is fleeing the other way. Where is he going to be when he is eighty years of age?

The matter has a more serious aspect than would appear from the really absurd character of the course which has been pursued by the Government and by the Prime Minister to-day. What is to be thought of public honour in this country if leaders of political parties are with impunity to be permitted to declare their faith to a nation, receive the votes of a nation and then with scorn, yea, with self-satisfied contempt, aban-10 p.m. don it immediately the responsibility of office is upon them? I know this is not the first instance. I also am pretty firmly convinced it will not be the last. I intend to hold myself in a position to complain if this wretched example is repeated, I purpose to be in a position to indict the administration. But there are many hon members of this House who will not be on very strong ground in that regard, who have already voted to absolve the ministry from obligations entered into with the people of this country. I am not in that position. And where is public honour to be in Canada if the people of this country when they come to exercise the sacred duty of voting are to have no knowledge at all of what are to be the principles that are to govern the administration when those they vote for are returned to power? I ask, are the people of this country after to-night to have any way in the world of judging as to what this Government may do upon any question whatever? If they are, by what talisman are they to be guided? Is there anybody in this country who can rest upon anything in the whole record of the administration and seize on that as a reason for saying that in his belief the Government will take any certain course upon any subject at all? I affirm that there is not. The Government has contemptuously and cynically turned its back upon every pledge made by its leader. On every one that has yet come before this House for discussion, it has cynically and contemptuously turned away, even when reminded of that pledge by one of its own most faithful supporters. That is the position in which Canada finds herself to-day, and is it any wonder, Mr. Speaker, that notwithstanding every opportunity given by the people, yea, and given by hon. members of this House, for the Government to establish itself by carrying out
column2: the

column1: Ministers and Directorships

task it undertook, by carrying out the programme it laid before the people-is it any wonder I ask that inches are coming off daily from the stature of the Government of this country, that it is going down in public estimation? The only explanation of the course they are taking now and have been taking ever since they ascended to office is that if they swerve from the course pursued by the late government to the right or to the left in the ruin they would precipitate the wrong they would inflict, they would bring the inches off their own stature faster than if they defied and entirely ignored their principles and declarations of the past. When hon. gentlemen opposite pursued lightly and without any regard to conviction, without any regard to argument, but merely for the sake of embarrassing the administration, as they thought, and of gaining a temporary advantage dear to the heart of the office seeker or the demagogue when hon. gentlemen opposite pursued lightly the lines of conduct they pursued a year ago, they could not but know that Nemesis surely would come. Doubtless hon. gentlemen opposite instigated the hon. member for Brome to bring in that bill of 1921, at least encouraged him to do so-

on December 6. The right hon. gentlemen seems to be sitting with his back to the engine, always looking at the scenery after he has passed it, but he will have to face the motive power of the machinery of this country, and look at things that we are approaching, and not at things we have passed. What we are called upon to do in this country, as a Parliament and Gov-

eminent, is what interests the people of Canada at the present time. During the campaign some of us made somewhat heated declarations. I think on this side of the House we are no exception to any of the hon. gentlemen on the other side in that regard. The people are reading the papers every day, not so much to know what we say to each other across the floor of the House, but to know what is being done to bring order out of the chaos which this Government found when it came to office.

The question before the House is one simply of practical business. I ask hon. gentlemen, if they were endeavouring to select men to conduct their business, and there were large financial matters of paramount importance to be discussed and dealt with, would they not seek for the men who had experience in those things? Every business man will say that is the correct policy. What is applied to our private business should be applied to our public affairs. The discussion to-day has been woven around the question of whether men who were able enough in a company to become directors of it might not do something wrong in a government. The fact that they have risen to become directors of a company, as my right hon. friend says, is something in their favour, because the men who know them best have entrusted to them their money to manage. That being the case, I take it, sir, that the people of the country do not make any mistake in passing the same kind of judgment. It is all very well for us to discuss a theory, and many theories that are not practicable are absolutely impregnable in discussion. I could name some of them, but will not. This is a question of practical every day business, and we should apply the best business intelligence we have to it.

Take, for instance, the resolution before us. How many hon. gentlemen in this House are shareholders in local rural telephone companies? A great many of them. Let me point out that the attempt to make this apply to directors who are ministers is merely drawing a herring across the trail. HOEY (Springfield) :,,MINISTERS AND DIRECTORSHIPS,,,Mr. Speaker, the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) is, in my humble judgment, a most important one, one the mere discussion of which will create widespread interest throughout this country, and one, the final outcome of which is awaited even now with considerable anxiety. My justification for rising to take part in this discussion is based upon the conviction that this proposal is, in spirit at least, in complete accord with British practice at its best,-British practice as exemplified and illustrated in the case of many outstanding leaders in Great Britain and, I am happy to state, by many outstanding political leaders in this country.

I should like to apologise to you, Sir, for introducing a personal element. I want to do so, in order to discover, if I can, the disease in the body politic, to which the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) has referred, and in order to come down into the realm of practical affairs, to which the Minister of Militia (Mr. Graham) has referred. During the recent federal campaign, an opportunity was ex-
Ministers and Directorships

tended to me to visit many constituencies in western Canada and one or two constituencies, at least, in western Ontario. During those visits I was astonished, shall I say alarmed and depressed, to find a large section of the Canadian people absolutely disinterested in the outcome of the election, not only in their respective constituencies, but in a Dominion sense?

I was naturally anxious to inquire into the cause of this apathy, and I learned that there was, amongst this section of the population, a widespread feeling that governments in Canada, from time to time, had been dominated, if not controlled, by the big interests of this country. I am not saying, at the moment, that they were right in this belief; I am only attempting, in my humble and awkward way, to interpret an attitude of mind. Let me say that I found this feeling most pronounced, not amongst the radical labour element and certainly not amongst the wealthy classes, but amongst what I might he justified in terming the better middle class, business men in a small way, professional men, teachers, many of whom were university graduates and all of whom were keen students of economic thought, the section of the population that, in the older countries, has always been able to determine the outcome of any election by throwing the weight of. its influence in with either of the two historic parties. I heard from this class again and again and again of the numbers of Cabinet ministers who, at the same time, were directors of large business companies. I heard them refer to politics as a game in this country, of profit only to those who occupied places in the inner circle. I heard, throughout that campaign, reference made again and again to campaign funds, and that reference to me seemed particularly pertinent when applied to the late government in the early days of the campaign and to the present Government in the closing days of that campaign. But the point that I wish to bring out is this, that that mysterious source from which campaign funds have been obtained in this country and the fact that there are directors of big interests occupying Cabinet positions, are inseparably bound up in the consciousness of a certain class of the Canadian people.

I made the statement then, which I repeat now, that unless something could be done to restore the confidence, and reestablish the faith, of this section in our political institutions, then the outlook in Canada was in no sense promising. We

have been witnessing during the past three or four years the collapse of constitutional government in more than one of the older countries. How has this collapse come about? I know whereof I speak when I say that in the case of one country that collapse was preceded by a century of propaganda that sought to convince the people that the government responsible for the administration of public affairs in that land was wholly dominated by the landlords and the wealthy men of Great Britain; and that propaganda, continued systematically, ultimately succeeded in completely undermining the faith of the people of that country in constitutional government. Turn to Russia and study its modern history and you will find that the collapse of constitutional government there was also preceded by a system of propaganda that sought to associate the government of that great country with the wealthy classes. It is my conviction that this impression, so widespread in Canada at the present time, that the governments of this country have been from time to time dominated by big business, has been created largely by propaganda for which all parties have been more or less responsible. That propaganda, in so far as it has substantial basis in fact, and foundation in truth, is commendable, believing as we do in the purifying influence of public opinion and publicity. In so far as propaganda of that kind is based on a desire for party advantage, however, it is pernicious and destructive, is always followed by disastrous consequences, and, in my opinion, is unworthy of the Canadian people.

I do not think he made any case at all. Before taking up the main argument on this question, I desire to indicate one or two points that should be considered in this motion if it is to pass at all. To begin with, the motion declares that ministers should resign their directorships on their appointment as ministers of the Crown. Well, Mr. Speaker, it would be very imprudent for ministers to resign their directorships on appointment to the Cabinet, especially had that applied to the ministers who were appointed shortly before the last general election. Several of those ministers never were elected to the House, and consequently had they resigned their directorships on appointment they would have resigned for no consideration whatever.
My hon. friend proposes further, that:
Such companies should have no business dealings with the Government of the Dominion of Canada, or with any department thereof, or with any railway or ship owned or controlled by said government;

It would not be fair to bar a company from doing business with the Government simply because one of its directors happened to be a minister of the Crown, because it is not within the power of a company to prevent its directors from entering the Government. The shareholders of a company generally elect their directors for one year, and it is not competent for those shareholders to displace any director within that period. Therefore I think that part of the resolution should disappear also.

That is supplemented by section 18, which provides that in every contract with the Government there shall be inserted a clause giving effect to the provisions of section 14. This law has been in force for about fifty years, and it has not been pointed out to-night wherein it has ever been insufficient. On the contrary, from all that has been said it appears that the statute has always been considered adequate and sufficient.

I suppose if this resolution should be accepted by the House it would be the duty of the Government to introduce a bill to give effect to it. But I say that this resolution in its present form cannot be accepted by the House, because it is arbitrary, uncertain, obscure, useless, and uncalled for. In a word, it has not been demonstrated that any evil now exists which a statute based on this resolution could remedy.

Now, let us examine some of the arguments put forward in support of the resolution. My hon. friend from Brome says that it is based on English practice. Well, I am sorry to differ, but I must say that that is by no means the case. On the contrary, that practice has been, making allowance for certain exceptions which only confirm the rule, that ministers of the Crown, do not resign their directorships. My hon. friend quoted the instance of the chairman of the board of directors of the Northeastern Railway Company, who on being appointed a member of his Cabinet by Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman resigned his railway position. But I submit, Sir, that that is not a parallel case at all, because anyone will readily understand that no man could hold the two positions concurrently. It would be about the same as if the President of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, or the President of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, when that company was a private corporation, were appointed ministers of the Crown. Therefore that case in my view falls within the exceptions that confirm the rule.

My hon. friend says, further, that it is a general practice for British ministers of the Crown to resign their directorships. Again I have to differ with him, and point out that not only in Great Britain but in Canada and the United States, generally speaking, ministers do not resign then-directorships on accepting portfolios. The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) quoted many examples of Min-
isters of the Crown since Confederation who accepted offices without resigning their directorship.

Now, in studying this question I think it is wise to refer to the law in other countries, and with that purpose in view I have examined the laws of Great Britain, the United States, and France, and in none of those three countries have I found any law that by any means resembles the statute which would have to supplement this resolution. I go further and say that in none of our provinces is there any such law in existence. If it is a good principle for the Dominion it is a good principle for the provinces, but, as I have just pointed out, none of the provinces so far has thought fit to embody the principle in legislation. In those three countries and in our provinces the rule has been to refer the question to the integrity, the honour and the sense of propriety of the minister so appointed. Now, sir, if that has been the standard in Canada for the last fifty years; if that is the standard in other countries, has that standard diminished in Canada of late? Is it since the present administration has assumed office that the standard of honour and integrity and sense of propriety has been lowered in Canada? Certainly my hon. friend from Brome will say ""No"" to that question, as I do myself. In a case like this, where it is more a question of propriety, good taste and honour than of law, I think the wish of the people should be considered. The wish of the people is a criterion, and when they elect as their representative one who belongs to any political party, knowing at the time of his election that he is director of a large corporation, they do so because they want that man to become a member of Parliament, notwithstanding his directorship in that corporation. Therefore I say that if the people want such men as their representatives in Parliament, who is going to say that they are not fit to become members? I apply my argument to members of Parliament because I contend that if my hon. friend's resolution has any foundation at all it must be applied not merely to ministers of the Crown, but to members of Parliament generally. Of course, being applied to members generally it would apply as well to ministers, the minister being only, after all, a member of Parliament. After a member has been elected by his constituents with the knowledge that he is a director of a company or large corporation, the Prime Minister may choose him as a member of his
Ministers and Directorships

ministry. The Prime Minister might or might not make an error in his choice, hut if he does make an error, if the people do not want this man to become a minister because of his directorship in a large corporation, the people have full opportunity of opposing his selection. After the member has been selected as Cabinet minister he must again go before the people for re-election; he must submit his conduct to them and be elected in his capacity as minister. Under those circumstances, when the people pronounce themselves twice, first by electing a man as a member of Parliament and next by re-electing him following his selection as a member of the Cabinet by the Prime Minister, then I say that Parliament should go no further.

It has been said that the work of a minister of the Crown is arduous and unremitting and that, therefore, he should give all his time to the duties of his office and entirely eliminate all other activities. But directorship in a corporation is only one of the many activities of mankind in which a member may be engaged, and if after becoming a minister a man is precluded from being a director of a corporation, he should also be precluded from looking after his own private business. He should be precluded from giving his time to any occupation whatever other than that pertaining to his office; and that would imply a severance from his friends, from all social functions, from his party affiliations, even from his family, if you want to go that far. Such was never the intention of government or of Parliament; such is not the intention of the people of this country. The people ask that a minister of the Crown shall give his best efforts to the work devolving upon him, but they do not and cannot reasonably ask that he abandon everything; that he should isolate himself, if need be, just because he is a member of the cabinet. It has been very properly pointed out that political life is often of short duration, and if after a man has worked for a lifetime and acquired some wealth he has to put it all aside in order to become a member of the cabinet, there is danger that the most able men in the country will, on that account, refuse to accept any such position.

The hon. member for Brome said, en passant, that no man could serve two masters. That is true, Mr. Speaker; no man can serve two masters if one be the Lord and the other the devil. No man can serve -two masters if they are antagonists; if they

are working on projects that are opposed one to the other. But in the ordinary course of life a man can serve two and more masters. A man can serve two masters if their interests are different. But any time a minister of the Crown thinks that the interests of the corporation of which he is a director may come into conflict with the interests of the Government; any time he feels that he is placed in a position where he cannot serve the two masters and he must decide between the two, it would be his duty to resign his directorship. Otherwise I do not see that a man who is a member of the ministry and at the same time a director of a corporation serves two masters in the biblical sense of the word.

The hon. member for Brome spoke very eloquently of what he called interlocking directorates. I submit that this resolution has nothing to do with interlocking directorates, if such things exist. What does it matter to this House that a member be a director of several companies if none of which has any connection or dealing with the Government? As long as there is wealth or riches in the country, men of prominence, influential men, men of wealth will be directors of companies, and in that there is no harm whatever?

The argument has been made to-night, and it is a good one, I think, that the fact of a man resigning his office as director of a company does not preclude him from retaining his interests in that company and from being represented by a dummy on its directorate. Suppose, for instance, that the director owns only a few shares in the company, having been elected a director because he was a capable and intelligent man, and that alongside of him there is a shareholder who owns a great many shares, but who is not a director because he is not as able as the other man. Is it not true that the large shareholder will have more interest in that company, although he is not a director, than the first man even though he were a director and a minister of the Crown ? Is it not true that the large shareholder who was not a director would be more concerned about the welfare of that company and more susceptible to influence than the director who owned only a few shares? Or take the case of a man who owns a large private industry and becomes a minister of the Crown. There is no reproach against him so far, but if he organizes that industry into a company and keeps a few shares",,,,

and becomes a director of that company, he could no longer be a minister of the Crown.

Parliament should always be very careful not to pass what I would call useless legislation. The object of legislation is either to procure a benefit or to cure an evil. I do not see that any benefit will be procured by the passing of the resolution of my hon. friend from Brome, nor do I see that any evil will be cured. If it had been shown that during the last fifty years under the present statute concerning the Senate and the House of Commons, evils had prevailed, or that minister of the Crown had abused his position, either in this or any other country, I would say that there was an evil to be cured, but nothing of the kind has been shown. On the contrary, when we know that ever since Confederation there have been in every government in this country ministers of the Crown who were directors of companies, it is wonderful indeed to think that no evils resulting from that situation can be pointed out to the House to-night. Therefore, I say that the safeguard which the resolution seeks to impose is an artificial, an imaginary safeguard. I believe that there is no necessity for it. What we want in the service of this country are able, experienced, business men, men in whom the community has confidence. Once a man has been elected a member of Parliament and is again re-elected as a minister of the Crown, I say that the confidence of the people of this country has been demonstrated enough so far as that individual is concerned, and for that reason he is fit to be a member of the Cabinet.

I heard one of my friends sitting in the party obliquely opposite make the argument tonight that men of large capital and influence who were directors of a company should not be allowed to become ministers of the Crown. We must be very careful about laying down any such principle as that. If we are going to accept as a principle that the rich man, the able man, the learned man, the man who has been ch'osen by his associates as president or director of a large corporation because they have confidence in him, is not fit to a be a cabinet minister, I would ask from what kind of material will your cabinet be drawn? There is a country in the world at the present time which has swept aside the rich and the powerful, directors of companies, let us say, and we know which country that is. While I would not by any

means compare what my hon. friend said to a Bolshevist utterance or the utterance of a demagogue, it reminded me of a story I saw illustrated by a cartoon not very long ago. Two policemen appeared with a prisoner before a judge in Russia, and were asked by him what was the charge against the prisoner. The policemen answered ""A capitalist."" The judge asked, ""What was he doing? How did you find out this man was a capitalist?"" The policemen answered, ""We found him in a barber shop having his hair cut.""",,,,

In conclusion, I wish to say that the principle at the bottom of this resolution is one which concerns the honour and the integrity of members of Parliament and ministers of the Crown, and I submit that the honour and integrity of a man cannot be remedied or improved by legislation. It is entirely a private matter concerning the honour and integrity of the individual. The people choose their representatives, and those who are chosen members of the cabinet have to go back to the people and accept their verdict.

One aspect of this question which has not been touched upon is that it is purely and simply a question of fact. It is not a question of law, it is a question of fact, and this is the distinction I would make between a question of law and a question of fact. If this question could be determined by a general principle of law applicable to all cases with equality and justice, then I would call it a principle of law. If we have to differentiate and to examine each case in particular, if the principle which is embodied in this resolution were true and right in one case, but might be unjust and unwise in another case, according to the circumstances, then I say it is essen-

tially a question of fact, and I submit that questions of fact cannot be regulated by statute. A question of fact has to be examined each and every time on its particular merits. That is the reason why it might very well happen in one case that a minister of the crown, being a director, could not remain in both offices without violating his oath of office. On the other hand, it might very well happen in many cases, and in most cases, that a minister of the crown could hold a position as director of a company without any incompatibility, without any evil or wrongdoing whatever, and, for that reason, I say that this question is merely one of fact. It cannot be regulated by statute, but can be regulated only by the sense of honour, integrity and justice of the man. For these reasons, I will vote against the resolution.

rise for the purpose of tendering, if I may, my respectful and heartfelt sympathy to the hon. member f.or Brome (Mr. Mc-Master). I think this is an occasion where he needs sympathy, where he deserves it and ought to have it in full measure. I am not in accord with the proposition which he has placed before the House. The party of which I am a member was not in accord with the proposition in its broader form when placed before the House last year. The hon. member for Brome will have no reproach to make to the members of the official Opposition. He cannot agree with them, but he knows that where they stand to-day they stood when he first introduced his resolution. He will, at least, give this portion of the House the credit for both sincerity and courage. Can he do as much for his own side of the House? For years hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House have accepted the services of the hon. member for Brome as one of the chief critics, if not the chief financial critic, of the Government of the day. He is a good Liberal and was brought up in the faith. He sat in council, though, as yet, I have not seen any very visible emblems of reward, and, perhaps, my hon. friend does not expect any, but, if I might paraphrase a little, I would have said that before the opening of this Parliament-at all events before the introduction of the resolution-he might have stood against the world. To-day there are none so poor in his own side of the House as to do him reverence. Every member of the Government and every supporter of the Government who has spoken
has, in a mild, perhaps charitable, but still possibly firm manner, told the hon. member for Brcane that he does not really know what he is talking about, and that his panacea is no panacea at all.

Unfortunately, some hon. gentlemen who took part in the debate this year, and also took part, even though a limited part, in the debate last year, and a larger number of them whc concurred in the vote last year, did not exrtess by their vote to the hon. member fo 'rome the things they say to him this year and the things they are going to show him by their vote tonight. It is rather unfortunate. He has been told that the principle is a good one, that no man can serve two masters, but I think the hon. member for Brome is probably considering it from a little different angle tonight. He is probably asking himself how one man can serve one master who goes in different directions at different times. The trouble is not in the multiplicity of masters, but apparently this chart, about which we hear so much, has come in evidence again-the chart that shows no lighthouse, no compass, nothing but an aimless sea of indirection upon which the political bark is allowed to float in a manner that will best serve the political exigencies of the moment. Let my hon. friend from Brome make up his mind now, a little late perhaps, to endure this sort of. suffering for the rest of his political career. He can now really appreciate the company into which he has gotten himself.

We have been told that public opinion is the master of this House. I hope so. I would be very glad to think that, and, , naturally, those of us who sit in this angle would like to lead public opinion along the same lines as we think, but how, may I ask hon. members of this House, are we going to do it? Shall we go on the public platform, or stand in this chamber, or discuss on the street, things that we do not intend to put into practice when we come into office? Shall we go from one end of Canada to the other, exhorting the people to support the Conservative party and declaring to those people that if we come into power we are going to do thus and so, and at the same time have the mental reservation that we do not intend to do anything of the kind, and that we intend to shape our course according to the expedience of the moment? That is not simply one of the issues, but that is the dominant issue in Canadian politics to-day, -whether the party shall or shall not be true to its previous record and true to the

pledges which it has given to the people. Shall we in this group follow the example, let me say the temporary successful example, which has been set? We intend to hold a nationwide convention of our party, to reassert and reaffirm those principles which eventually will he triumphant in this country. And when we do so, are we to take as a guide that great convention w! 'ch was held a few years ago, the party Dehind that convention having, up to th .me, practically repudiated or refused to put into force every plank, every doctrine, in the platform to which it subscribed? My hon. friends, who sit to my left on this side of the chamber, in fact, I might say, the party which is in morganatic alliance with the Government, a truly morganatic union because it gets none of the honours and yet it is expected to bear its share of the burdens of this entanglement, have supported this morganatic union by voting in this House to absolve, so far as they can, the gentlemen who have gone to the country on one platform and who have come back to this House to put into practice an entirely different platform. The morganatic alliance will be a splendid institution while it brings the necessary support to a government that cannot live without it. It will be utterly disregarded when it interferes with the interests or desires or prejudices of hon. gentlemen who sit to the right of Mr. Speaker.

I should like, just for a moment, to deal with what the Minister of Militia (Mr. Graham) said. I think he referred to the fact that the party on this side of the House was a defeated party, and his satisfaction is quite evident, quite natural, quite pleasurable. The hon. gentleman should not be too hard upon defeats. I fancy it was only the fact that he too had been defeated that prevented him from joining in the chorus and vote which supported the hon. member for Brome last year, and he probably would have been as busily engaged as other members of the Government to-night in swallowing his previous utterances if he had been a member of the

House last year. Fortunately, he had escaped, and he was able to take what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) and, in fact, pretty nearly every hon. gentleman who has spoken to-night believe is the wise, sane and healthy course; for I believe myself that the rewards in political life are all too small to induce the captains of industry to enter political life and give their services to the state, and instead of putting up barriers to keep such men out, I believe it is in the interests of the country that such men should be induced by every possible means to come in and help administer a government. I find no fault with the Prime Minister for having induced such captains of industry, such capable businessmen as he has, although the number is not, by any means, as large as it might be for the good of the country.

I can assure my hon. friend the Minister of Militia (Mr. Graham) that defeats are not permanent. We are in the posi-iton of a party which, when it again meets the country, will present to that country an unbroken record of consistent adherence to what we, at all events, have believed, do believe, and shall believe, is the best policy in the interests of the entire country. When my hon. friends go to that country for endorsement, it will be utterly impossible to tell from their previous performances what their next performance will be, whether they will go back to the platform they discarded or adopt something new. But this will be sure, that whatever they may utter on the public platform, in the discussions of the next campaign, whatever they may print in their handbooks, whatever they may set forth in the newspapers of the country, will, on the word of the Prime Minister, be nothing more than an advertising campaign to get votes, and will not entail, in their eyes, any obligation upon a single man jack of them to carry it out after he gets back to the House. And my hon. friends to my left can take credit to themselves for having voted to endorse that particularly responsible and, I was almost going to say, that particularly honest statesman.

Now, what the people in this country vote for, that they will get. What their representatives in this Parliament vote for, that they will get. And if they vote for sham and insincerity they will have it in full measure; but they will not get it from this group. My hon. friend from Brome
Ministers and Directorships

(Mr. McMaster) last year made a declaration, and in tones of most respectful sympathy. I want to commend to him the careful study of his words. Hansard records him as saying: ""I know my own leader and can speak for him."" Can he tonight? Did his wildest imagination a year ago ever foresee the day when his honoured leader would rise in his place and repudiate him and his resolution, and swallow whole, without an effort at gulping it, the doctrine promulgated last year by my right hon. friend the leader of the official Opposition (Mr. Meighen) ? And does the hon. member for Brome think that that is distinctly a good thing in Canadian public life? Is it the sort of thing he wants to subscribe to? It is the sort of policy any man can pursue? Would it not have been at least decent, would it not have been at least fair, to have given the hon. member for Brome some notice of a change of direction, some notice of the back-tracking of the Government, so that he could at least get into line in the procession if he wanted to? That would have been more merciful than to treat an old stalwart supporter to the kicks of absolute repudiation, when he is standing for what he at any rate believes to be an absolute principle and absolute right.

625392,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.12.27,1922-04-24,f0d1049a-4acc-4789-a93f-b3bceae69e3f,ca.m.8624,Mr. WILLIAM IRVINE (East Calgary) :,,EDITION,,,The hour is rather late, but I believe that this issue is of sufficient importance to warrant the few minutes I shall devote to its consideration. The member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) in his resolution, and in his most excellent presentation of the case, has given voice to a sentiment and emphasized a principle which I feel sure will receive very hearty endorsation from the people of the country. I wish to congratulate him on his splendid courage, and on the wisdom and moderation which he exhibited in the presentation of his arguments. ""Behold a Liberal indeed, in whom is no guile.""

I have been rather surprised, however, in the debate which has followed, that patriotism has not been emphasized very much. I do not think there is any class in Canada that is more apt to wave the flag and to prate about patriotism than parliamentarians in general, and we have not to look very far back to find where hon. gentlemen, who have taken part in this debate, waved the flag until the folds were almost worn out. But here is an opportunity for practical patriotism. This resolution calls upon the man of ability, who has proved that ability in the affairs of business, to give his service to the country, not his half-hearted efforts but his whole-hearted service, as well as his complete time, for which the country pays him and is grateful. And yet, not one single parliamentarian has lifted up his voice or waved the flag on this occasion. Surely this is worthy of patriotic emphasis.
Ministers and Directorships

Most of us agree with the central thought of the resolution, that no man can serve two masters, and that we are called upon to vote as to whom we will serve, or as to which master we wish to see our administrative representatives serving. It is very clear-and this is the point which has withstood the test of argument, for no one has challenged it so far as I have heard- that when a cabinet minister holds the position of director in any company he cannot give all his time to the service of the country, while at the same time there may be a clashing of interests. For this reason it is well that he should separate from one or the other, that he should be called upon to give his services in a patriotic sense to the nation, or else give his whole time to the industry which has claimed his attention so far.

I think it was the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) who submitted that no harm has been done by this old method. What an argument indeed! Have we been reduced to a miserable negation? Is that the only argument that the hon. member can put forward in support of his position? He very well knows that it is exceedingly difficult to prove whether any harm has been done in a direct sense; but, nevertheless, I am not so sure that we cannot prove in a general way that harm is being done and will be done. We have just had a bank collapse, and, as 1 understand it, one of its directors was a member of the late administration. He admitted that he had been giving attention to the Government and not to the institution that collapsed. Now, is it not reasonable to suppose that if he had been attending to the bank's business he would have known the condition it was in and would have warned the public, or perhaps even saved the institution? There is a case at least where harm did come. Is it not harmful where a man is so divided in his interests that he cannot give good service to one or the other?

No one will deny that throughout the country there is prevalent an idea that the financial interests, the railway interests, and the manufacturing interests have in the past had a very great deal too much to do with Canadian governments. As to whether that very settled opinion is well founded or not is another question, but the fact remains that a very large section of our people entertain it. Consequently, if we passed such a resolution as this, and implemented it with legislation, it would
to some extent remove the ground for that opinion at least, and tend to establish greater confidence in administrative bodies.

If a corporation represents a man's life, as the hon. member for South Wellington put it, let that man stay with that corporation; there is no particular demand that he should give it up. Then the hon. member tried to give this argument a personal turn and mentioned specifically the hon. Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin), who, he warned us, was the actual foundation of the present Government and who, if this resolution passed, might resign. I do not know the hon. member's authority for that statement, but personally I do not think that eventuality would be possible. I am willing to admit the greatness of the hon. Minister of Justice. I believe that every hon. member recognizes his ability, and would regret very much anything that would deprive him of the opportunity of serving his country at this time. But it is just because we believe in his greatness that we have no fear in passing this resolution, for surely such a great man as we believe him to be would not, because of a statutory prohibition, as it was termed by the Prime Minister, feel called upon to resign. We believe that the hon. Minister of Justice is too big a man to take such a course; on the contrary, we believe he would be patriotic and continue to serve his country notwithstanding such legislation. No one would imagine for a moment that the hon. minister would fail to rise to the opportunity for patriotic service afforded by this resolution. But let me put it another way: What would the people think of the hon. Minister of Justice if he should resign because this resolution was passed? There is the other side of the question. I do not believe they would think very much of him if he did resign; personally I think he would say: I have been selected to serve my country at a very critical time in her history, and I am going to rise to the patriotic level of this resolution and continue my services for the benefit of the nation.

Now, the hon. Prime Minister went around so many corners in his swift retirement from his previous position that I was not able to keep my eyes upon him, and consequently I cannot follow him in all the turnings he made. The argument which he so ably delivered to-night I am sure could have been delivered a year ago with equally good reason. If the argument put forward to-night is good, it was good a
Ministers and Directorships

year ago. I believe this is another evidence of the influence of the party system. Either the Opposition to the late administration were wrong in supporting that resolution, or they are wrong now in refusing to support it. In the one instance the Prime Minister was in opposition; now he is in power. Did the Prime Minister vote for a more drastic bill last year to give assurance to the electorate, as he put it, or did he vote for it to discredit the government then in power? Which was the reason then, and what is the reason now? Personally I regret very much that he feels it to be his duty on this occasion to back away from that position, for I do not think it will be taken as a high example by the young men of this Parliament that our Prime Minister so suddenly has forgotten the argument of his party and his own vote and stultified himself on this occasion. I do not think anyone who reads the argument in Hansard-if anyone ever troubles to do so-will feel that he has justified his action satisfactorily, if he was right last year, and I want to say again that I regret very much that he has seen fit to take this action on the present occasion.

The Prime Minister also referred to the practice in Great Britain. I should like to find out if there has been a single case in the last forty years where a member of the British Government has found it necessary to resign from the directorate of any company. If that is not so, what is the reason? Is it not that the members of the British House of Commons do not expect to be called to office if they hold directorships?

The hon. gentleman also made much of the defeat of Swift MacNeil's resolutions in the British House of Commons. Does he not know that they were voted down by Tory majorities? And is that the standard the Prime Minister of a Liberal Government sets up in the twentieth century? I hope it is not. Perhaps he overlooked that.

Then the leader of the Opposition of course comes along to make political capital out of this; and I think perhaps we were as tired of his argument as we were of the argument of the Prime Minister on this question. There is really no credit coming to the leader of a Tory party for not having moved,-because he cannot move. Everyone knows that that is an impossibility, for if he were moving he would not be a Tory, he would have to be something else. He is this year where he was last year; he will be there next year
and all the years that are to come. And when he places himself right straight in the middle of the road of progress, we all know there is no necessity to make a long speech about it.

Next the hon. the Minister of Militia (Mr. Graham) comes along, and he is very anxious to forget all about last year. No one blames him for that of course; that is quite human; I think I would want to forget it also. He told us that the argument of the hon. member for Brome un-forunately came from the upper regions. Are we to understand that the answers to his argument come from the lower regions? I can see no other conclusion-and really, they sounded like it.

Then came the member for St. John and Albert (Mr, Baxter) swimming an uncharted sea without destiny or direction; and he begins by presuming to give the full interpretation of the resolutions that are passed in this House.

ments have not been touched. Hon. members who have spoken in opposition to it have brought up various arguments from their point of view, but I think that it will be agreed that those who wade through Hansard to-morrow will find the argument of the hon. member for Brome unanswered; it stands tier upon tier just as he built it up. That is the issue, and I believe the people of Canada expect us to vote for this resolution.

625397,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.12.32,1922-04-24,4472d34d-ab33-4491-a84f-4c3450223604,ca.m.7304,Mr. H. A. FORTIER (Labelle) (Translation) :,,EDITION,,,Mr. Speaker, I want to state first that I am opposed to the resolution of the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) and I wish to give this House my reasons for this opposition. This resolution, I believe, implies a departure from constitutional usage, and any legislation which might be adopted following this resolution would result in depriving the Cabinet of the services of a distinguished citizen, whom the people of his province and county entrusted with their confidence and, who is absolutely needed under the present circumstances for the good administration of Canada.

In fact, Mr. Speaker, if this resolution were adopted, that person, who enjoys the confidence of his fellow-countrymen would have no other alternative but to choose between the directorates conferred upon him by important companies and the distinction of being a minister of the Crown. Given such a case, the man who possesses the confidence of every one, would likely choose the directorates; and this is why it would be deplorable for our country to behold men so highly necessary and endowed with such intellectual powers, cast aside; it would be a misfortune indeed, if such men were denied all participation in the administration of public affairs. It would be detrimental to our country, and this is the reason why I shall not support this motion. I am convinced that the resolution of the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) is uncalled for and in support of my contention, I may say this. In the first place the country needs the services of able and intelligent men for the good administration of the country's business. The world over, able statesmen are scarce and when we do happen to possess such

men, they should be called upon to take an active part in public affairs. In most cases, however, they have already been designated by their fellow-countrymen to fill the important directorship of these large financial companies. This entirely shows their remarkable aptitude and skiil and it is incumbent on the country to entrust to them the management of public affairs. If this resolution were adopted, Mr. Speaker, we would be deprived of the benefit of having amongst our administrators men of experience and ability.

Secondly, in any constitutional government, there is a sacred duty which imposes itself upon a Prime Minister, the one of personally choosing his colleagues. But by this legislation you prevent the Prime Minister from calling upon those who are on these important directorships and who are highly qualified; you circumscribe his freedom of choice which it is most important should remain unimpaired, and you tell him: when you are selecting your Cabinet, you shall not be allowed to single out men who are directors of large companies; you shall have to ignore them; you shall have to choose men in whom you have not an absolute confidence, men who have not given proof of integrity and long experience.

My last argument is this: the purport of the resolution is to cast odium on the public man of the day. How? Because this man has private or personal duties to fulfil, you believe he is not broadminded enough, when his country requests his services as minister of the Crown, to so engross the time in a disinterested manner; because this man has a pecuniary interest in a company, you throw open to doubt his love for his country. I repeat it, I believe this resolution is based on a false principle. I had no intention to take part in this discussion, but I changed my mind after listening to all the arguments which were brought out during this debate, especially to those put forward by the opposition and to those brought out by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Baxter). He stated that, not being a member of this House last year, he takes his cue in supporting the resolution, from the attitude then taken by his leader. For my part, I do not believe that we are inconsistent with our past in voting down the resolution of the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), and this is why I deemed it my duty to make known to this House the reasons that have induced me to take such a stand.
