625398,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.12.33,1922-04-24,b518c3e0-9d1a-43c2-8a1e-a14029b83b97,ca.m.4509,Mr. J. L. STANSELL (East Elgin):,,EDITION,,,My only justification for speaking on this resolution at this late hour is its importance and the dearth of argument that has been submitted in its favour. To me this has been an evening of astonishment, not the least part of which was the statement a few moments ago by the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Johnston) who, turning to this corner of the House, said that if his party ever got into difficulty they would not come to us for help, because we did not change. That statement was made in spite of the fact that only a few members in this corner of the House had spoken on this subject. He followed that up by saying in his next breath that men may come and men may go, but he and the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) were going on forever. They never changed. I submit that if the hon. member has no more faith in our party and its desire to help forward anything that we believe to be in the interests of this country than he has in his own consistency, I do not blame him very much.

I believe this is a particularly important question to those of us who are in Parliament for the first time. Speaking for myself, I am not inclined to form a hasty opinion upon a subject of this kind. I looked for instruction, for inspiration, if you like, from those who were friendly to the measure. My only source of information has been the record of the debates of last session, which show that fifty-four members of the House were strongly in favour of this measure and voted for it a year ago. Strangely enough they are nearly all in one group to-night and prominent among them is the Prime Minister himself and many of his Cabinet. I had expected that the right hon. leader of the Government would give us some information in support of this measure which he advocated a year ago and let me point out that there is no argument against this resolution that was not just as applicable twelve months ago. As the right hon. leader of the Government has said he did not speak at any great length on this question a year ago. May I be permitted to quote a few sentences from one who is held in very high esteem not only by the Prime Minister himself and his party but by all parties and members of this House? The Prime Minister himself in his eulogy on' appointing this hon. member to the position of First Commoner, spoke of his exceptional ability, his great endowments and his distinguished public service. In view of the well known modesty of the

hon. gentleman who holds that high position I shall mot refer to him more personally, but I am sure he will pardon me if I quote just a few sentences of his remarks in the debate on this question of last year, and which I am sure the Prime Minister himself applauded and concurred in. On page 592 of volume I of last year's Hansard I find this:

I say is not the honour of being a minister of the Crown, the honour of being sworn in as a Privy Councillor, a reward by itself? In my humble judgment, no man should hesitate, when accepting that honour, to put aside his private interests ... I say that it is in the interests of the ministers of the Crown, and of good government and of the good reputation of Parliament that public opinion should be satisfied that there are no conflicting interests between ministers as such and any directors of private concerns. . . It strikes me, after having heard my hon. friend and the objections that were made by some of the hon. gentlemen on the other side-mild objections I must say-that this is a needed reform and one which is consistent with British traditions.

Surely 'in view of such a careful and well-worded pronouncement on this important subject, we could not look for anything but support of this resolution upon the part of those who were friendly to the measure last year. Among those to whom I particularly looked for guidance is the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie), the Solicitor General. I particularly looked to him because I had the pleasure of hearing him a few nights ago, when I was very much pleased with his eloquence and ability. Moreover, his apt quotations from Scripture show that he is at least in touch with a very high authority. So much was I impressed with his eloquence that I was not surprised, on looking up last year's debate to find that he used the words "" Wash us and we shall be whiter than snow."" I presume that in the meantime he has not forgotten the tune. That may not be necessary now; as it would have to be changed anyway to wash us over again, because to my surprise I find that some who advocated this measure a year ago have fallen from grace, not the least being the Prime Minister himself. I had expected that the hon. member for North Cape Breton would use his missionary powers and great ability in endeavouring to convince those of us who are new members, and are in a sense sitting in darkness, not to mention some of the older members who perhaps have exhibited somewhat sceptical tendencies. I seem, however, to be doomed to disappointment because evidently his time and abilities will be taken up in per-
Ministers and Directorships

suading the leader on his own side of the House. My hon. friend is very apt in quoting Scripture, so no doubt he remembers the parable of the ninety-nine sheep that were safe in the fold but one was wandering on the moun-12 m. tainside, and it is well-known what anxiety that caused. What, then, can we say on this occasion, when although there are ninety-nine safe in the fold, one is lost in the wilderness, and that is the bell-wether, the leader of the flock. Surely, if missionary work is necessary, it is necessary on that side of the House, and we on this side of the House will probably be denied the privilege of that much-needed persuasive power.

I might also have looked for enlightenment to the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe), who last year supported this measure. We all know his undoubted ability and eloquence although he has not been particularly generous to the House in that respect this session. I had hopes that he had been reserving his powers in order to try and get this resolution carried by a large majority. Perhaps it is not too late yet for the hon. member for North Cape Breton to secure assistance from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries in endeavouring to convince those of us who need information and are in a sense still wandering in darkness.

Speaking seriously, there are something like one hundred and thirty new members in this House, who are anxiously looking to those who have been here and understand the needs of the country, and are in a position to give direction and guidance to those of us who are learning. Are we to be told by the fifty-four members who voted in favour of this measure last year, that the facts and arguments they made in support of it then are not now to be taken seriously? Surely any arguments that could be made in support of the measure last year are equally applicable to-day. Surely now, when the sun of democracy is shining and responsible government has again been restored, we may look for stronger and better guidance in the future.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,John Lawrence Stansell,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b518c3e0-9d1a-43c2-8a1e-a14029b83b97&Language=E&Section=ALL
625399,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.12.34,1922-04-24,b4773d7c-fb30-477a-9d14-c076e60905ac,ca.m.9274,Mr. T. L. CHURCH (North Toronto):,,EDITION,,,I did not intend to speak upon this debate, but after what has been said on the subject I would like to say a few words. This is private members' day, but I think it should be called Brome day. The speech of the hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King)
should be enough to let the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) know that his friends have all forsaken him and fled.

The principle embodied in this resolution is an academic one. I do not know what object the hon. gentleman has in introducing the motion. He cannot accomplish anything by it because if it is carried it will not have any effect and will merely be a scrap of paper. The privilege which has been attacked by the resolution has not been abused by the late government nor by the present Government, and I think the present Government should be given a fair show. There are only one or two members of the Government holding directorships. I think the Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin) was one of the best provincial premiers the province of Quebec ever had. I am sorry he is not here to-day. Judging from what he has done for the municipalities he has accomplished more than any previous premier ever did. He has erected court houses, registry offices and other public buildings for the municipalities in his province. He has done more for the municipalities of the province of Quebec in this connection than has been done in any province of the Dominion.

If there was ever a time in the history of this country, both in Dominion and provincial affairs when the country wanted business men, it is the present. In my province of Ontario we have a government without a single business man in it. Look at the loans they have made and the financial statement in the budget brought down in the Ontario legislature. They say they have a surplus, but nearly a million of maintenance charges has been put into capital. That is the way they run the province. The privilege dealt with in this resolution has not been abused by the present Government. One or two of the ministers hold some directorships but the passing of this resolution will not mean anything to them. They will not lose any directorships by it.

I may say to my hon. friend from Brome, and my friends, the Progressives, that if they went a little farther up than the mere directorships it would be better for the country and the proposition would commend itself to the judgment of the country. Let them take up the question of the banks and their business methods. Let them deal with the question of the Merchant's Bank which had a president who did not preside, directors who did not direct, managers who did not manage and auditors who did
Ministers and Directorships
not audit. If that matter were investigated something might be accomplished for the country in that direction.

This motion would not prevent shareholders in these large concerns from becoming members of Parliament or Cabinet ministers and probably a large shareholder would be far more injurious to the company if he were in the Cabinet than a director could. The motion does not refer to corporation lawyers and legal counsel. Can they too be retained in the Cabinet to the exclusion of those who are directors? This principle has been discussed in England and it has not been adopted there. They leave the matter to the honour of the ministers. I think we have a very honourable body of ministers here. The Prime Minister must be a responsible officer and has very responsible duties to perform. The ministers work in the mornings, afternoons and evenings. I do not know what time they get to attend to their own affairs or the affairs of any company with which they might be connected. I do not think that the privilege I have referred to has been abused. The principle of the motion may be all right in some respects, but there is no demand for it in the country or in the House, and I do not understand why the time of the House should be taken up with it. The Minister of Justice has given up directorships in La Presse, in The Cockshutt Plow Co. of Brantford, a six million dollar concern, and one or two others, I think. I believe we might leave this matter to the ethics and to the honour of the gentlemen of the Cabinet. There is no demand and no necessity for the resolution and I do not see how any good can come of it. I hope the House will not take up any more time and I ask that the vote will be taken.

Mr. JOSEPH T. SHAW (West Calgary) : I think, with all due deference to the member for North Toronto, (Mr. Church) who has just preceded me, that this matter is one of vital importance to the people of this country. I am not concerned as to whether or not the attitude of the Prime Minister is due to what I might term conscientious inconsistency, or perhaps due to party exigency, nor yet am I concerned with the problem of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) as to whether he is standing to-day where he stood yesterday, and where he proposes to stand in the future. It seems to me the hon. gentleman from Brome (Mr. McMaster) has presented to this House a very important and very essential principle, and that, in the
[Mr. Church.!
discussion which has taken place, and the desire to make party capital out of this situation, we have ignored the question at issue.

The first thing I should like to direct attention to is the fact that the resolution, as compared with last year's resolution, is very much narrower and is confined to what I might call public service corporations, using the term as used by the good people to the south of us. These corporations are the ones which must, of necessity, come frequently to this Parliament, and must very frequently make applications which are passed upon, approved, or disapproved by this Parliament. For instance, the railway companies are under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission. The cabinet, the executive of this House, sits in appeal from that Railway Commission from time to time, or may do so. Then take the situation with regard to banks; these institutions are, as one writer has stated, the manufacturers of credit on other peoples' money; they must, at regular intervals, make reports to the Finance Minister, and those reports are subject to inspection by this parliament from time to time. Not only that, but I believe it is the practice every ten years to revise the Bank Act under which they operate. Then again, we have insurance companies, which also are peculiarly under the jurisdiction of Parliament. That, to my mind, is the distinguishing characteristic between the corporations mentioned in the resolution and the private corporations which were included in the resolution of the hon. gentleman from Brome introduced last year. These, as I say, are public service corporations. They are corporations which are performing public functions, and, in that sense, they are perhaps performing a duty of government.

What is the position of a director in one of those companies? He stands, of course, as a trustee for the shareholders. It is his duty to advise on matters of policy, to direct the government and to preserve and to enlarge, if need be, the assets of his company. On the other hand, what is the position of a minister before this House? And I, from my standpoint, see absolutely no distinction between the position of the first minister of the Crown and that of any other Cabinet minister. He is here simply as a trustee, entrusted, perhaps, for a short time or, perhaps, for a longer period with responsibility from his constituents and from this House. He is the trustee of the people and the executive
Ministers and Directorships

trustee of this Parliament. Under those circumstances, if a man occupies a dual capacity, as a director in a public service corporation and, at the same time, as one of the executive of this House, with the necessity, as I suggested at the outset, for supervision or inspection of his company at various times and in various ways, is it not possible that, at some time or upon some occasion, his interest as director may conflict with his duty as trustee of this House? That, I take it is in short, the neat point for discussion now, and the question is not one of whether somebody took a position six or twelve months ago inconsistent with the position now assumed. That is a matter of special significance, perhaps, at a time like this when institutions, including even this institution in common with all other governmental institutions, are being questioned and analyzed as never before by the people at large. It is absolutely essential that the independence of Parliament should be preserved; that there should not be even the slightest breath of suspicion regarding the conduct of any minister of the Crown in connection with his relation to any private or public corporation.

It is the plain duty and responsibility of this House to see that no one shall be put into such a position of difficulty by having to act in a dual capacity, and if he is, by circumstances, put into that position, then he should resign the directorship or his position as a minister of the Crown. Not only is this in the interest of Parliament itself; but, to my mind, it is equally in the interest of the corporations affected. These corporations have, perhaps, secured much money on the strength of the particular members mentioned as directors. Men of every class and walk in life are, perhaps, expecting, and reasonably so, that these particular individuals as directors will give all their time, energy, and talent to the care of their corporations. Not only are their interests involved; but the interests, perhaps, of hundreds of other people are likewise involved. Therefore, it occurs to me that, while it is a proper thing for a minister upon his appointment to resign his directorships, I think we should have on the statute books of Canada legislation affirming this resolution, so that no one can be put into that dual position. We should divorce private interest from public duty, by a statutory prohibition of this Parliament. I shall, therefore, have much pleasure in supporting the motion of the hon. member for Brome.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Thomas Langton Church,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b4773d7c-fb30-477a-9d14-c076e60905ac&Language=E&Section=ALL
625400,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.12.35,1922-04-24,ee1cc492-9867-48d3-a612-c1fb491d2916,ca.m.1883,Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Centre Winnipeg) :,,EDITION,,,Mr. Speaker, may I direct attention to just one point, to which, I think, attention has not yet been called, and that is the absolute necessity that there should exist in this country some body that will protect the people from the arbitrary power of these great corporations? Within the past few years, as we all recognize, there has been a shifting of power from the political to the industrial field. In the olden days, when industry was a small affair, the employer had comparatively little power. To-day, when industry is on such a large scale, the employer has power such as those in political power know nothing whatever about. We sometimes have talked of captains of industry, of princes of finance, of money kings. These terms are significant of a real state of affairs, because, in many respects, the men, who are at the head of our big industrial, commercial and financial affairs, have more real authority than those who occupy prominent positions in the political life of the country. It has been stated that whoever controls a man's job-I am speaking as a Labour man- controls his life. That is true; whoever controls a man's job, controls his very livelihood, and if he has no one who can stand between him and arbitrary power, his case is perfectly hopeless. Within the last few years we have witnessed a great concentration of capital in this country, so that to-day the big financial institutions determine whether or not there shall be production; they determine in what branch of industry there shall be production, and upon what terms that production shall be carried on. That being the case, it seems to me that it is absolutely essential that, in some way, there should be an impartial authority absolutely dissociated from those big interests, which can protect the people of Canada from the arbitrary power which those industries have gradually attained.

The hon. member for Brome (Mr. Mc-Master) referred to a chart which had been prepared and which showed the interlocking directorates to which he made reference. He gave no names of directors, giving only the numbers, doing this in order that no personalities might enter into the discussion.

,Labour,,James Shaver Woodsworth,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ee1cc492-9867-48d3-a612-c1fb491d2916&Language=E&Section=ALL
625401,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.12.36,1922-04-24,deaf5a4f-d8a1-49b8-a81b-f90eeaf06463,ca.m.9018,Mr. McMASTER:,,EDITION,,,Was that not a wise thing?

,Liberal,,Andrew Ross McMaster,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=deaf5a4f-d8a1-49b8-a81b-f90eeaf06463&Language=E&Section=ALL
625402,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.12.37,1922-04-24,ee1cc492-9867-48d3-a612-c1fb491d2916,ca.m.1883,Mr. WOODSWORTH:,,EDITION,,,It may have been a wise thing. I can quite understand the position of the hon. member for Brome.
Ministers and Directorships

As, however, the discussion has gone on, reference has been made to the one member of the cabinet who is included in the list given by the hon. member for Brome. Some days ago I was furnished, not by the hon. member for Brome, but by a friend who had evidently been working on the same proposition, with a graph of this character, based, I believe, upon the Canadian Annual Financial Review of June, 1921. It seems to me that a graph of this kind ought to be placed definitely before the people of Canada, and they would then have no doubt as to the absolute necessity of this body making some provision for preventing power being placed in the hands of a few men such as we have here. As the hon. member for Brome was reading the list, I was checking this particular graph with his, and I think it is the same graph as it represents the same figures, the total capital controlled being something like $4,295,000,000. The names of the fifteen men who each have directorship in from two to eight of these big companies or corporations are as follows: 1, Sir Augustus Nanton; 2, Sir John Aird; 3, Sir Edmund Osier; 4, Lt.-Governor Cockshutt; 5, E. W. Beatty; 6, Sir Vincent Meredith; 7, Baron Shaughnessy; 8, Sir Lomer Gouin; 9, Sir Herbert Holt; 10, Sir Charles Gordon; 11, .C. R. Hosmer; 12, Hon. R. Dandurand; 13,
J.
column2: E. Aldred; 14, C. E. Neill; 15, E. L. Pease.

column1: It seems to me there is no particular reason, if these men are occupying the most honoured positions in the country, why their names should not be generally known to the public, in order that their position in society should be recognized. I quite realize the fact that they have attained this position because of considerable business ability and all that kind of thing. It is not a matter of impugning their personal integrity in any sense whatever, but it is a question as to how the public itself can in some way control the great power which has gradually been concentrated in the hands of a comparatively small group of men. The resolution of the member for Brome would look to the separation of the Cabinet, on the one hand, from the power which is exercised by great corporations on the other. That may be a temporary measure; but it is in the right direction. The public generally is not going to be satisfied until, in some way, not only do we insist that Parliament shall not be directly controlled by these great corporations, but that, on the other hand, in some way, right within the corporations themselves, there shall be in-

troduced a very large measure of democracy. Political democracy was the watchword of the last generation, and we are all glad to think that we have attained a certain measure of political democracy. But political democracy is an absolutely hollow thing unless we have industrial democracy as well. This resolution which has been presented to day is simply the first step in controlling these great aggregations of capital which have placed almost unlimited power in the hands of small groups. For that reason I believe I am expressing the opinion of a large group of at least the labour and middle class people in this coun. try when I urge that the resolution be adopted.

,Labour,,James Shaver Woodsworth,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ee1cc492-9867-48d3-a612-c1fb491d2916&Language=E&Section=ALL
625403,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.12.38,1922-04-24,deaf5a4f-d8a1-49b8-a81b-f90eeaf06463,ca.m.9018,Mr. McMASTER:,,EDITION,,,I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I will not be long in my closing remarks, but there are just a few things which I think, in justice to myself, and I hope, in the interest of the country, I should say. I will deal with the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). In his eloquent observations he made the statement that I had wrongly interpreted the practice in Great Britain, and that in 1896 a committee of the House of Commons had sat for the purpose of considering the question whether it would be wise to more stringently draw the rules of the House of that great Parliament along the lines of, although not quite precisely in accordance with, my resolution of to-night. It is quite true that it was decided not to change the rules of that House, but that decision was arrived at by a vote of six to five. The five that voted for the purpose of amending the rules, more in the spirit of the resolution I have before the House to-night, were, Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman, Mr. Courtney, Mr. Haldane, Mr. Lloyd George and Mr. MacNeill, while those who were opposed to any change were Mr. Bonsor, Sir W. Hart-Dyke, Mr. Halsey, Mr. Grant Lawson, the Solicitor General and Mr. Woodhouse. Now, I respectfully suggest that the five who voted in support of the principle I now advocate are well worth the six on the other side.

The Prime Minister stated that I had no ground for believing that anything untoward had happened in connection with his administration, and I would assure you, Mr. Speaker, I would assure him, I would assure this House, and I would assure this country, that I never suggested for one moment that there was anything untoward in any action of this Government. In bringing this matter before the House, what
Ministers and Directorships

have I done? I have simply done what I did last year with the enthusiastic co-operation of the Prime Minister himself. Not only in the debate which has been referred to, as to the advisability of directors in large companies being ministers of the Crown at the same time, but in another debate, was the attitude of the party plainly set forth. There was that debate provoked by me in connection with the railway estimates, in a speech which I made showing the inadvisability of members of the board of directors of the National Railways being also members of the board of directors of any company who might sell things to the railway. It was not precisely the same case, but it was precisely the same principle; for what is the principle? Without imputing wrongdoing to any one, I say that the principle is that a man should not be put in a position where either his personal interest or his fiduciary interest can conflict with any other fiduciary interest. That position was assumed by me on that occasion. I made a speech then late in the evening, and the Prime Minister did me the great compliment of placing largely the same facts before the House in his own budget speech. He did me the further compliment of placing those facts before the country from the Atlantic to the Pacific.

,Liberal,,Andrew Ross McMaster,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=deaf5a4f-d8a1-49b8-a81b-f90eeaf06463&Language=E&Section=ALL

The case of members of the board of directors of the railways purchasing for the railways from companies on the boards of which they are also directors, is not parallel to the principle now under consideration. If similar action were attempted by a minister of the Crown he would be disqualified in five minutes.

,Liberal,,William Lyon Mackenzie King,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5&Language=E&Section=ALL

of millions.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Arthur Meighen,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=d02a7b53-dad0-4944-82b0-aed9054a7bc2&Language=E&Section=ALL
625408,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.12.43,1922-04-24,deaf5a4f-d8a1-49b8-a81b-f90eeaf06463,ca.m.9018,Mr. McMASTER:,,EDITION,,,If I might interject myself into the debate, if I remember the circumstances correctly, and I think I do, it was not charged by me or by the Prime Minister that directors of the national railways who were directors in other companies had been selling. The point I made was that they belonged to companies which might sell, and therefore it was improper

for them to be also directors in the national railways, who might buy from the companies in which they were concerned. There was a possibility of a conflicting fiduciary interest. Now, let us take the question of banks. I do so frankly, and I would point out to the House that I was careful in my introductory remarks to avoid any personality at all. It is a principle that I am advocating, and I try to keep away from personalities altogether. Let us put the case in a supposititious way. Suppose there were a minister of the Crown who was a director in a bank. Suppose that bank were doing work for the government. Do not even suppose that; suppose the bank were only doing what banks are obliged to do every month, sending in returns to the government. Suppose my right hon. friend were in power; what position would he take in regard to his Minister of Marine and Fisheries, say, when it was found that the bank of which he was a director had to be charged with having sent in false returns to the government. What position would my right hon. friend be in, and what position would his Minister of Marine and Fisheries be in if such a situation existed? I do not need to stress the point, Mr. Speaker. The thing is so patent that it is inadvisable to have ministers of the Crown directors also of banks.

Now, I spoke about interlocking directorates. The Prime Minister said: Well, interlocking directorates should be treated as such. I ask: By whom? By this Parliament, which may contain certain members in the Cabinet who are also members of these companies whose directorates interlock? It seems to me that whatever our opinion may be about the advisability or inadvisability of interlocking directorates, we should see to it that the interlocking does not pass into the Cabinet chamber. That is the position I am putting before the House to-night; I think it is reasonable.

It is true the Prime Minister seems to think that there is plenty of protection in the Senate and House of Commons Act, extracts from which he quoted. Now, if there was not an exception-which he did not read-permitting a company of which a member is a shareholder, dealing with the Government, what he said would, I think, be quite accurate and the necessity for this resolution would to a certain extent disappear. But it seems to me that whether a man is a director or merely a shareholder in the company, the fact that he is such does not prevent the company from dealing
Ministers and Directorships
with the Government. I think that is a correct interpretation of the law.

Shareholders need not give up their shares; that is quite true. I am sorry that I seem to find myself in the unfortunate position of not being able to please anyone. Last year my right hon. friend situated angularly opposite said that my resolution went too far, and now my critic seems to think that my motion does not go far enough.

,Liberal,,Andrew Ross McMaster,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=deaf5a4f-d8a1-49b8-a81b-f90eeaf06463&Language=E&Section=ALL
625409,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.12.44,1922-04-24,d02a7b53-dad0-4944-82b0-aed9054a7bc2,ca.m.4870,Mr. MEIGHEN:,Leader of the Official Opposition,EDITION,,,My hon. friend is looking in my direction. I did not say that. I took objection to it on principle as not meeting the case at all.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Arthur Meighen,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=d02a7b53-dad0-4944-82b0-aed9054a7bc2&Language=E&Section=ALL
625410,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.12.45,1922-04-24,deaf5a4f-d8a1-49b8-a81b-f90eeaf06463,ca.m.9018,Mr. McMASTER:,,EDITION,,,I stand corrected

then. But last year I remember my right hon. friend saying: Why, you are trying to imp y that a minister should not even have the interest that his family gives him. And I recollect saying, with the former Minister of Trade and Commerce, Sir George Foster, in front of me, that it would be impossible to impose celibacy on his government. Shareholders need not give up their shares; that is quite true. I am not going on the assumption that there is something wrong. If there are dishonest men in public life, they will be dishonest no matter what legislation is passed; but what I do say is that we should try to prevent a possible conflict of fiduciary interest. The Prime Minister has said that leaders of political parties should not accept directorships. I agree with him. But I do not agree with him if he sets a higher standard for himself than for members of his government, because my view is that all the members of the Government, especially in view of our constitutional principle of solidarity, stand more or less on the same footing-that the Prime Minister is merely primus inter pares.

My hon. friend stated that my resolution would deprive him of the ability of leading business men. Now, that is exactly contrary to what I wish by my resolution. If first class business men go into the Cabinet, I wish them to be absolutely ""off with the old love before they are on with the new"" .-I wish them to be in a position to devote 'their whole time and attention to the affairs of the Government. I am of opinion that men of ability, no matter how rich they are, will be glad to do this if they have the proper spirit which we wish to see manifested in our public men.
The Prime Minister implied that in bringing forward this resolution I had
[Mr. McMaster 1
given way to a sentiment of juvenile audacity; that I should leave such questions for older and wiser heads.

,Liberal,,Andrew Ross McMaster,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=deaf5a4f-d8a1-49b8-a81b-f90eeaf06463&Language=E&Section=ALL
625411,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.12.46,1922-04-24,b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5,ca.m.7719,Mr. MACKENZIE KING:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs,EDITION,,,No, I was speaking entirely about myself.

,Liberal,,William Lyon Mackenzie King,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5&Language=E&Section=ALL
625412,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.12.47,1922-04-24,deaf5a4f-d8a1-49b8-a81b-f90eeaf06463,ca.m.9018,Mr. McMASTER:,,EDITION,,,That just shows how one may misunderstand even one's friends. I must no longer detain the House. I have merely one argument to make, and that is in reply to stmething said by the right hon. leader of the official Opposition. He said: Under this resolution proposed by the member for Brome you might have in the Cabinet men representing the British Empire Steel Corporation and the Dominion Textile Company; that there is nothing to prevent great industrial corporations having their directors in the Cabinet; and the member for Brome says that that is all right. Of course, my right hon. friend sometimes exaggerates.
column2: I

column1: never said that that is all right. I grant that that abuse is not specifically covered by this resolution. I grant the difficulty of keeping out certain companies and saying that the directors of those companies should not be in the Cabinet. What I have done is to pick out those classes of companies the directors of which have a particular fiduciary relation to their shareholders; thus the banks look after the money of the people, the trust companies look after the estates of the people. The companies I have picked out are large companies, companies which are very powerful and whose operations affect the whole people. It is possible that my resolution does not go far enough, but I say it is a step in the right direction and I trust it will meet with the approval of this House.

625418,ca.proc.d.1922-04-24.14.2,1922-04-24,89103d9d-627c-4f56-8113-57b0d3865982,ca.m.3867,Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance) :,Minister of Finance and Receiver General,ANNOUNCEMENT OF NEW CANADIAN LOAN,,,"Before the House adjourns, may I be permitted to announce a very important financial transaction which has just been closed. The Government have sold $100,000,000 of Canadian bonds to Messrs.
J.
column2: P. Morgan and Company of New York. The bonds will be placed on the market tomorrow at par, bearing interest at five per cent, for a thirty-year period, callable after twenty years. The Government, of course have to pay commission to the banks, but the bonds will be offered to the public to-morrow in New York.
